title: Enterprise Multi-Agent Reliability

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

notes.takeaway: Interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning with tool actions so a model can plan, query external sources, and self-correct — reducing hallucination on decision tasks.
notes.why: The base pattern under most single agents. Reliability work below is largely about what happens when you compose many ReAct-style agents and the failure modes that emerge.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation

notes.takeaway: Framework for composing customizable agents that converse, integrating tools and humans to solve tasks collaboratively.
notes.why: A representative conversation-topology framework. Treat the topology it lets you express as a design + security decision, not a default — see the topology and security pillars.

papers.title: Is Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) the Silver Bullet? Empirical Analysis in Code Summarization & Translation

notes.takeaway: Structured multi-agent debate yields minimal-to-inconsistent gains over a strong single-agent baseline on software-engineering tasks.
notes.why: The headline reliability finding: fan-out is not free quality. Adopt multi-agent only where it beats a measured single-agent baseline on YOUR tasks.

papers.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST failure taxonomy)

notes.takeaway: 14 failure modes in 3 categories — specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, task verification — built with an LLM-as-judge pipeline at Cohen's κ=0.88.
notes.why: A ready-made vocabulary for incident review. Label your own failures against it — but treat the taxonomy as a living checklist, not a frozen schema (models change, failure modes shift).

papers.title: Beyond the Strongest LLM: Multi-Turn Multi-Agent Orchestration vs Single LLMs

notes.takeaway: Consensus-topology ablations: visible authorship raises self-voting and ties; visible live vote tallies raise herding and premature consensus.
notes.why: If you run review/debate quorums, blind the lanes and hide interim tallies by default — visibility measurably biases the consensus toward the wrong answer.

papers.title: λ_A: A Typed Lambda Calculus for LLM Agent Composition

notes.takeaway: Well-formedness / termination guarantees for agent composition via a typed calculus.
notes.why: Formal guarantees are appealing, but the realistic enterprise failures are config typos (nonexistent agent refs, empty templates). A cheap install-time validator usually beats a type system here.

papers.title: TraceFix: Repairing Agent Coordination Protocols with TLA+ Counterexamples

notes.takeaway: Uses TLA+ counterexamples to repair coordination protocols.
notes.why: The formal-verification angle on coordination. Worth knowing exists; for most teams a configuration linter + good traces catch the protocol bugs that actually occur.

papers.title: Robust Agent Compensation (RAC): Teaching AI Agents to Compensate

notes.takeaway: A log-based recovery layer intercepts each tool call, records a transaction log (pending/completed/failed/compensated), retries transient errors, and rolls back completed dependents by reverse-topological compensation — no agent-code rewrite. Materially cheaper than replanning.
notes.why: Recover from logs, not by re-reasoning the whole plan. Keep a per-run transaction log and a compensator per side-effecting tool; recovery cost then scales with failures, not plan size.

papers.title: ACRFence: Preventing Semantic Rollback Attacks in Agent Checkpoint-Restore

notes.takeaway: Checkpoint/restore duplicates irreversible effects (double commits, double payments, token reuse) unless the tool boundary enforces replay-or-fork: replay a recorded response when equivalent, require an explicit fork for a new irreversible op, block consumed-credential reuse. LLMs regenerate subtly different requests even at temperature 0.
notes.why: The single most under-appreciated agent reliability bug: a retry after a side effect lands repeats the side effect. Idempotency keys + replay-or-fork on every external write are table stakes.

papers.title: SagaLLM: Context Management, Validation & Transaction Guarantees for Multi-Agent LLM Planning

notes.takeaway: Brings database-style transactional safeguards — checkpoints, compensable execution, compensation pairs, global validation, rollback — to multi-agent planning.
notes.why: Names the right mental model: treat a multi-step agent workflow like a saga. Compensation + validation are the load-bearing parts; the planning DAG is optional.

papers.title: Toward Autonomous Long-Horizon Engineering for ML Research (AiScientist)

notes.takeaway: 'Thin control over thick state': a durable shared workspace holds artifacts, plans, experiment records, failures, and diagnoses while a lightweight orchestrator invokes specialists as tools. Ablating the durable workspace or the hierarchy hurts.
notes.why: Pass durable references between agents, not chat summaries. A shared task/artifact store survives context loss and crashes; conversational handoff does not.

papers.title: An Agentic System for Rare Disease Diagnosis with Traceable Reasoning (DeepRare)

notes.takeaway: Nature paper: a host decomposes the case, invokes specialized servers, self-reflects, and emits ranked outputs with evidence-linked rationale. Validated on 6,401 cases with blinded expert review of the reasoning chain, not just final answers.
notes.why: In regulated/high-stakes settings, capture evidence references and a validation summary so a human can review the reasoning chain — auditability is a first-class output, not an afterthought.

papers.title: Shepherd: A Runtime Substrate Empowering Meta-Agents with a Formalized Execution Trace

notes.takeaway: Makes agent execution a first-class object — a structured effect stream (model calls, tool calls, fs/env changes, commits, branches, fork points) that can be inspected, forked copy-on-write, replayed from a changed point. CooperBench joint pass 28.8%→54.7% with a meta-agent; suffix replay reuses the shared prefix + prompt cache.
notes.why: Transcripts are not observability. A structured, replayable execution trace is the substrate under debugging, evaluation golden sets, and any supervisory/optimizer layer. Build it first; almost everything reads off it.

papers.title: AgentSight: System-Level Observability for AI Agents Using eBPF

notes.takeaway: Defines useful agent observability as correlation between high-level intent (LLM traffic) and low-level action (syscalls, file/process events), joined by time + process lineage. <3% overhead; exposes multi-agent coordination bottlenecks invisible to either stream alone.
notes.why: Correlate intent with action, not just log prompts. The join catches reasoning loops, prompt-injection exfiltration, and hidden coordination bottlenecks. Prefer standards-based telemetry over a bespoke tracer.

papers.title: AgentForge: Execution-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Autonomous Software Engineering

notes.takeaway: Validates correctness by actual program execution in a resource-bounded, network-isolated sandbox — plan → minimal patch → synthesize tests → run → debug → validate before propagation. SWE-Bench Lite 40.0% (+26–28 over single-agent/ReAct); both execution feedback AND decomposition ablate as load-bearing.
notes.why: Ground evaluation in execution, not model likelihood or simulated feedback. Run candidate work in a sandbox and gate propagation on the result.

papers.title: A Multi-Agent Coding Assistant for Cloud-Native Development (CloudMAS)

notes.takeaway: Reports compile-success / test-pass / deploy-success / API-consistency, stratified by task complexity, with token + cost + time accounting. (Preprint; single underlying model is a validity threat.)
notes.why: For software workflows, measure the things that actually fail in production — compile, test, deploy — with cost per task, stratified by difficulty. One headline accuracy number hides the reliability story.

papers.title: AI Assurance: A Comprehensive Testing Strategy for Enterprise AI Systems

notes.takeaway: An enterprise testing strategy: failure taxonomy, assurance pyramid, eval lifecycle, model/RAG/agent governance. Probabilistic systems can't be proven correct; product readiness ≠ benchmark score.
notes.why: Frame eval as risk reduction, not proof. Tie controls to a recognized governance framework and keep a sample under human review.

papers.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains

notes.takeaway: Benchmarks agents on multi-turn tool use plus a dynamic simulated user in retail/airline domains, scoring reliability over repeated trials (pass^k).
notes.why: Closer to enterprise reality than single-turn QA: it measures consistency across trials, not a lucky single run. Reliability is a distribution, not a point.

papers.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?

notes.takeaway: Tests whether models can resolve real GitHub issues by generating patches validated against the repository's own test suite.
notes.why: The canonical execution-grounded benchmark. Its design lesson: let the existing test suite be the oracle, so the eval can't be gamed by plausible-looking output.

papers.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

notes.takeaway: Establishes LLM-as-a-judge, validated against MT-Bench multi-turn questions and crowdsourced human-preference rankings — and documents the judge's biases (position, verbosity, self-preference).
notes.why: LLM judges scale eval but are biased. Calibrate against human labels, report agreement, and never treat a judge score as ground truth.

papers.title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data

notes.takeaway: Trains routers on human-preference data to dispatch between strong and weak models, cutting cost while preserving quality.
notes.why: Routing can be learned from data — but it needs real cost/quality signals. You can't route on cost you don't measure; instrument first.

papers.title: CascadeDebate: Multi-Agent Deliberation for Cost-Aware LLM Cascades

notes.takeaway: Escalates from cheap to expensive models only when deliberation signals uncertainty — a cost-aware cascade rather than always-on fan-out.
notes.why: Recent confirmation that a cascade is the cheaper shape than parallel fan-out for deliberation. Gate escalation on uncertainty signals you can compute.

papers.title: Minions: Cost-Efficient On-Device ↔ Cloud Language-Model Collaboration

notes.takeaway: Splits work between a cheap local model and an expensive cloud model to cut cost while holding quality.
notes.why: Tiering across a local/cloud boundary is a concrete cost lever — useful where data residency or latency also matter.

papers.title: Autellix: A Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs

notes.takeaway: Treats agent programs as first-class scheduling units, improving throughput/latency for agentic workloads.
notes.why: Scheduling is its own reliability surface: bound per-step time so one slow check can't stall a whole batch, and schedule at the program level, not the request level.

papers.title: Node-Sampling: Adaptive Multi-Agent Optimization in Medical Education

notes.takeaway: Learns a policy over agent-call sequences with a length-regularization penalty and a STOP node; a regularized 3-agent sequence uses ~1/3 of the fixed-baseline calls.
notes.why: Adaptive selection works but is domain-specific. Record route/outcome/cost facts first; optimize selection from data, don't hand-author a routing table.

papers.title: Orchestrating Human-AI Teams: The Manager Agent as a Unifying Research Challenge

notes.takeaway: Formalizes workflow management over a task-dependency graph with workers (capabilities, availability, cost rates), hard/soft constraints, and graph-modifying actions. Reactive managers that over-assign and under-inspect fail.
notes.why: Expose the task graph + resource facts to operators. Good orchestration inspects and decomposes; it doesn't just dump work onto workers.

papers.title: DynTaskMAS: Dynamic Task-Graph Asynchronous/Parallel Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Builds dynamic task graphs executed async/in parallel instead of a static schedule.
notes.why: Prefer dynamic DAGs for heterogeneous, data-dependent work — model dependencies explicitly and let independent branches run concurrently.

papers.title: APWA: A Distributed Architecture for Parallelizable Agentic Workflows

notes.takeaway: A distributed architecture for fanning out independent agentic workflow steps.
notes.why: When work is genuinely parallel, a distributed fan-out architecture pays off — but only after you've confirmed the steps are independent (a barrier kills the benefit).

papers.title: From Skills to Talent: Heterogeneous Agents Organized as a Company (Dynamic vs Fixed Roles)

notes.takeaway: Heterogeneous agents form dynamic rather than fixed roles, organized like a company.
notes.why: Keep roles in config/prompts so they can form dynamically. A hardcoded class hierarchy of agent types ossifies and resists the next model upgrade.

papers.title: A 2-D Framework for AI Agent Design Patterns (Cognitive Function × Execution Topology)

notes.takeaway: Classifies agent design patterns along cognitive-function and execution-topology axes.
notes.why: A useful vocabulary for design reviews — name your pattern on both axes before building it, so you choose topology deliberately rather than by default.

papers.title: MPAC: A Multi-Principal Agent Coordination Protocol (extends MCP + A2A)

notes.takeaway: A coordination protocol for multiple principals, extending tool (MCP) and agent-to-agent messaging.
notes.why: When multiple owners/principals share an agent fabric, the coordination protocol is also a trust boundary — design who can address whom explicitly.

papers.title: Learning to Communicate: End-to-End Optimization of Multi-Agent Language Systems

notes.takeaway: Treats inter-agent communication as something to optimize end-to-end rather than fix by hand.
notes.why: Frontier/research: the content agents exchange can itself be tuned. Today, keep communication in prompts and optimize from eval data, not a learned protocol baked into infrastructure.

papers.title: LLM-Skill Orchestration: Rule-Augmented Multi-Model Collaboration

notes.takeaway: Low-confidence preprint: decomposes tasks into skill graphs executed by heterogeneous models with rule-augmented orchestration; same-model parallelism alone underperforms heterogeneous execution.
notes.why: Provider heterogeneity is worth evaluating as config/eval metadata. Resist turning 'skills' into a rigid registry — keep model choice in configuration.

papers.title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising LLM-Integrated Apps with Indirect Prompt Injection

notes.takeaway: Attackers compromise LLM-integrated apps by planting instructions in content the model later retrieves (web pages, documents) — no direct access needed.
notes.why: The defining agent threat: any retrieved content is potential attacker-controlled instructions. Treat tool/RAG output as untrusted input, always.

papers.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: A dynamic benchmark of realistic tool-using tasks for measuring prompt-injection attacks and defenses — and showing current defenses are far from complete.
notes.why: Put injection benchmarks in CI. You can't claim a defense works without an adversarial eval that tries to break it.

papers.title: Red-Teaming LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Communication Attacks

notes.takeaway: Injects malicious messages that propagate through inter-agent communication channels, compromising a multi-agent system from the inside.
notes.why: Injection doesn't stop at one agent — it propagates. One agent's output must not silently become another agent's command. Validate and least-privilege every inter-agent message.

papers.title: Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security

notes.takeaway: The same task under different multi-agent architectures has different security properties.
notes.why: Topology is a security decision. Choose who can dispatch to whom, and who reads whose output, for the attack surface — not just for performance.

papers.title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: Benchmarks LLM multi-agent collaboration and competition across coordination topologies with milestone-based KPIs, not just final-answer accuracy.
notes.why: If you run multi-agent, evaluate the collaboration itself — coordination quality and topology effects — not only whether the final answer was right.

papers.title: Preference Leakage: A Contamination Problem in LLM-as-a-Judge

notes.takeaway: Shows LLM judges systematically favor outputs from related/sibling models — a contamination bias that silently inflates evaluation scores.
notes.why: If your judge model is related to the model under test, your eval is contaminated. Use independent judges, human-anchored samples, and report the risk.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM-based Agents for Multi-Turn Conversations: A Survey

notes.takeaway: A structured (PRISMA) survey of evaluation methods and benchmarks for multi-turn LLM agents.
notes.why: A map of the agent-eval landscape — useful when choosing or assembling an evaluation suite rather than reinventing one.

papers.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions

notes.takeaway: Surveys the security threat landscape of MCP — the tool-connection standard now powering most agentic systems — and its expanding attack surface.
notes.why: Every MCP tool you connect widens the attack surface. Inventory and least-privilege your tool/MCP connections; treat the protocol layer as a trust boundary.

papers.title: AgentShield: Deception-based Compromise Detection for Tool-using LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: Plants deception traps (fake tools/credentials) that detect indirect-prompt-injection compromises which slip past prevention — cross-lingual, near-zero false positives.
notes.why: Detection complements prevention: rails will miss some injections, so add tripwires that fire when an agent does something it shouldn't.

papers.title: G-Safeguard: A Topology-Guided Security Lens and Treatment on LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Detects anomalies over the agent communication graph and intervenes to defend a multi-agent system against attacks that propagate between agents.
notes.why: Monitor the inter-agent communication graph itself for anomalies — the topology that carries work also carries compromise.

papers.title: CARROT: A Cost-Aware Rate-Optimal Router

notes.takeaway: Routes each query to the cheapest model that still meets a quality bar, with rate-optimality guarantees.
notes.why: The modern cost-router: set a quality floor and let routing minimize cost beneath it — but it needs real per-model cost/quality measurements to work.

papers.title: Harnessing Multiple Large Language Models: A Survey on LLM Ensemble

notes.takeaway: Taxonomizes LLM ensemble and routing strategies — before, during, and after inference — for combining multiple models per query.
notes.why: A reference taxonomy for deciding how (and whether) to combine models: route, cascade, or ensemble, each with different cost/latency/quality trade-offs.

papers.title: RouteNLP: Closed-Loop LLM Routing with Conformal Cascading and Distillation Co-Optimization

notes.takeaway: An enterprise closed-loop router using conformal cascading + distillation co-optimization, reporting six-figure monthly inference-cost reduction.
notes.why: A concrete enterprise routing case study: closed-loop routing with statistical (conformal) guarantees can cut inference spend materially at scale.

papers.title: MemReader: From Passive to Active Extraction for Long-Term Agent Memory

notes.takeaway: Actively extracts and populates long-term agent memory rather than passively logging, improving the reliability of personalized long-horizon agents.
notes.why: Long-horizon reliability needs deliberate memory, not just a growing transcript. Treat what an agent remembers as a managed, durable store.

papers.title: OpenTelemetry — Semantic Conventions for Generative AI & Agents

notes.takeaway: An open, vendor-neutral standard for telemetry from LLM and agent systems — spans/metrics/events for model calls, tool calls, token usage, and agent operations.
notes.why: Adopt this as your trace schema so observability is portable across vendors and tools. It is the closest thing to a common substrate for the execution traces the research above argues for.

papers.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

notes.takeaway: A voluntary, widely-referenced framework organizing AI risk management into Govern / Map / Measure / Manage functions.
notes.why: Map your agent controls to a recognized framework so 'reliability' becomes auditable. Pairs naturally with the assurance + governance research above.

papers.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications

notes.takeaway: A community-maintained catalogue of the top LLM-application security risks — prompt injection, insecure output handling, excessive agency, supply chain, and more.
notes.why: The practical security checklist for agent systems. 'Excessive agency' and 'prompt injection' map directly to the topology and injection findings above.

papers.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context (DeLM)

notes.takeaway: Coordination is state-based, not prompt-routed: intermediate progress persists as compact verified gists in a shared context that later agents read directly, instead of being rewritten into successive prompts and rebroadcast by a controller.
notes.why: The recovery branch's thesis that durable state beats conversational handoff — DeLM makes progress survive as reusable problem state rather than living in transient prompt chains.

notes.takeaway: Built on two global structures — a shared context C and a task queue T; agents claim ready subtasks, and when the queue empties the last finisher decides whether to enqueue another round: a dynamic task graph rather than a fixed plan.
notes.why: The topology branch's preference for dynamic task graphs over static orchestration; DeLM shows the decentralized queue+context topology outperforms centralized scatter-gather on SWE-bench.

papers.title: SWE-Marathon: Can Agents Autonomously Complete Ultra-Long-Horizon Software Work?

notes.takeaway: Scores 20 project-scale software tasks with multi-channel hidden verifiers (dense test suites, behavioral parity against a reference, performance gates, deterministic replay, audit checks, and computer-use UI judges) plus a no-op-fails / oracle-passes solvability gate and adversarial exploit search at construction time; across 1,300 rollouts 10.2% ship a verifier bypass yet the layered defense catches all 132, so none earns reward, and frontier agents still resolve under 30% at pass@1.
notes.why: The eval branch's thesis that evaluation must be grounded in execution against an honest baseline — SWE-Marathon refuses single-test grading, anchors each task to a human reference solution, and treats reward-hacking resistance as part of task construction rather than a post-hoc filter.

notes.takeaway: A 5-bucket failure taxonomy over 526 agent-attributable failures: implementation failure (41.6%) and timeout (31.4%) dominate, then reward hacking (15.4%), premature termination (7.6%), and poor self-verification (4.0%); long context degrades behavior actively — pass rate falls monotonically with consecutive-duplicate run length (claude-code 41.9%→3.2%) and compaction/summarizer trials pass at 0% vs 8.9% without.
notes.why: The reliability branch's insistence on knowing the failure taxonomy before scaling — at hour-scale horizons the binding constraints are sustained self-verification and idle-loop degradation, not raw capability, and more tokens and compaction track failure rather than rescue it.

papers.title: XFlow: An Executable Protocol Programming System for Reliable Multi-Agent Workflows

notes.takeaway: XFlow treats actor outputs as proposed values that become shared state only after schema validation, provenance recording, and commit-policy checks; updates are atomic transactions that roll back the symbol store on failure, and committed changes mark derived values stale for recomputation. Sessions persist as scoped frames (visible symbols, pending outputs, event-log positions, blocked human gates) plus the symbol store and event log, so execution resumes from durable state, not from replaying an informal transcript, and operators can audit who proposed a value and why execution is blocked.
notes.why: This is the recovery branch's thesis made executable: durable, queryable, transactional state with rollback beats conversational handoff, and side-effecting steps sit behind commit gates rather than control-flow retries over free text.

notes.takeaway: The paper makes the failure taxonomy explicit before scaling fan-out: a single agent's hallucinated/malformed/misinterpreted output becomes shared state and corrupts downstream decisions. Concrete failure modes observed: tau3-bench baseline reaches the right end state via an invalid path (treats a parameter clarification as authorization to mutate); CorpusQA fails on the interpretation rule not the retrieved value; SWE-bench baseline submits a patch after local validation already failed. The cloud-edge fan-out is gated: edge workers see only assigned chunks, write only declared outputs, and must pass schema + coverage checks before entering global state.
notes.why: Directly answers 'does fan-out help?' (only when each parallel branch's output is schema/coverage-validated before merge) and supplies a named failure taxonomy (invalid-path success, rule-misapplication, premature submission) to know before scaling.

papers.title: Knowledge-Based Zero-Replay Debugging of Multi-Agent LLM Traces

notes.takeaway: The system compiles each raw multi-agent trace (messages, routes, memory writes, tool calls, decision events) into a typed event knowledge graph: nodes are events, edges encode routing and causal adjacency, and the attribute map assigns each node route-graph position, memory/retrieval persistence, tool-call metadata, uncertainty proxies, and optional latent payloads. Every downstream component operates on this graph rather than raw text, so the evidence behind each debugging decision is explicit and auditable. Cheap CPU features extract in milliseconds per trace; the predictor adds no LLM call.
notes.why: This is the concrete instantiation of 'transcripts are not observability': flat logs only become debuggable once recompiled into a structured, replayable representation that correlates intent (routing/decision events) with action (tool calls, memory writes) and exposes which events are causally adjacent.

notes.takeaway: Evaluation is grounded in a deterministic counterfactual-replay oracle (leave-one-out remove-event ablation scoring outcome-distribution shift plus state and trajectory divergence), locked across all 37 trace families (163,815 events) as reference truth. The authors explicitly call it intervention-relative, not absolute causal ground truth, and calibrate with Spearman rho, AUPRC, NDCG, reliability bins and ECE (linear scorer ECE=0.13) so low-confidence recommendations can escalate to active replay. The predictor recovers ~80% of the active-replay oracle's recall at zero replay cost; on Who&When the LLM-free CPU model matches an RL-fine-tuned 8B LLM while the benchmark's own zero-shot LLM judges reach only <=0.14.
notes.why: This is eval as risk reduction, not proof: an honest execution-grounded replay oracle rather than an LLM judge, a refusal to claim universal dominance (centrality wins 15 families, learned predictor 18, 4 ties), and a direct calibration check on whether LLM judges can be trusted for failure attribution.

papers.title: SEAGym: An Evaluation Environment for Self-Evolving LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: Evaluation is grounded in execution: SEAGym builds on Harbor (containerized task execution, verifiers, parallel jobs) and separates task rollout from method update, so diverse self-evolving agents connect through thin wrappers while keeping their native update rules. Instantiated on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and HLE comparing ACE, TF-GRPO, and AHE under a shared epoch/batch protocol, it shows frequent updates may fail to improve held-out performance and that useful intermediate snapshots can collapse later.
notes.why: It models the branch's stance that evaluation must be grounded in execution against an honest baseline and treated as risk reduction rather than proof: verifier-checked task outcomes plus held-out and replay views surface regression and non-transfer that an aggregate success score would hide.

papers.title: AgentArmor: A Framework, Evaluation, & Mitigation of Coding Agent Failures

notes.takeaway: Decomposes non-adversarial coding-agent failure into three sequential points — forming the correct target (underspecification), pursuing it (capability error), and executing it through the harness (stochastic sampling, context decay) — with a chain-rule risk P(unsafe)=1-(1-f1)(1-f2)(1-f3) and scenarios that isolate each stage, cross-cut by four active modes (greenfield, editing, deployment, monitoring) over 8 scenarios, 20 environments, and 59 transcript templates at n>=500 across three frontier models.
notes.why: The reliability branch is about knowing the failure taxonomy before you scale. This gives a deployment-grounded taxonomy of where a single coding agent goes wrong and measures each stage's failure rate separately, instead of reporting one aggregate success number.

notes.takeaway: AgentArmor is a harness modification, not a better base model: deterministic guardrails (force ls -la before deletes, read scripts before executing), a LoRA-trained command classifier with a '3 strikes' policy and persuasion-blindness to resist goal drift, and self-harness tools (user-overridable immutable files, transcript pruning) that cut unsafe and irreversible actions by a statistically significant margin.
notes.why: Security here is governance over the agent's action surface. AgentArmor shows that runtime guardrails and an intent-aligned command classifier, rather than model scale alone, are what actually block destructive commands like rm -rf and DROP DATABASE.

papers.title: Lingering Authority: Revocable Resource-and-Effect Capabilities for Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: PORTICO is a reference monitor that gives coding-agent tools a bounded capability lifetime: an explicit task contract compiles into an initial envelope plus grant, trusted-closure, and global-deny rules, and a request-grant-invoke protocol mints opaque, epoch-bound handles that are revoked when the subgoal closes, so authority cannot linger or be replayed once its justifying episode ends.
notes.why: The security branch treats the agent's exposed action surface as the attack surface. PORTICO argues that least privilege over time matters as much as sandbox reachability: in their audit it rejected 10/10 post-closure capability reuses and executed 0/6 stale forbidden writes where a non-revoking comparator with the same grants allowed all of them.

papers.title: RigorBench: Benchmarking Engineering Process Discipline in Autonomous AI Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: Names a failure taxonomy for the lab-to-production gap — fragile fixes (patches pass tests but leave latent bugs), token waste (trial-and-error instead of a planned approach), false confidence (never abstaining on impossible/ambiguous tasks), and broken intermediates (codebase left broken between steps). Baseline ReAct agents fail badly against it: no baseline abstained on any of the 6 impossible tasks, and even disciplined agents abstained correctly only 62% of the time. Recovery is the hardest mode and the one scaffolding does NOT fix — smallest gain of all five pillars, token-waste cut only 34%, doom loops persist when root cause isn't in the error message; the authors conclude recovery may need architectural changes beyond configuration-level frameworks.
notes.why: The 'know the failure taxonomy before you scale' point made concrete: the paper names how agent systems fail silently in production and shows the hardest failure mode — error recovery — is exactly the one a harness does not buy you, so scaffolding is not a substitute for the underlying capability.

notes.takeaway: Scores execution traces, not final artifacts: it logs every plan, diff, command, per-action token count, and timestamp, then scores five pillars (Planning Fidelity, Verification Coverage, Recovery Efficiency, Abstention Quality, Atomic Transition Integrity) into a weighted RigorScore. The design uses an honest control — four harnesses (Agent-Rigor, Agent-Skills, Superpowers, Baseline ReAct) on the same model and same 30 tasks, 120 executions — isolating the harness effect rather than asserting it. RigorScore correlates with outcome quality at r=0.87 (p<0.001), and qualitative sub-metrics use a 3-judge majority panel calibrated at Fleiss' kappa 0.74. Process discipline raised process scores 41% and outcomes 17%.
notes.why: This branch's thesis — execution-grounded eval, an honest baseline, calibrated judges, eval as risk reduction — is the paper's entire method: it replaces outcome-only pass@k with trajectory scoring, attributes gains against a real control, and measures judge agreement instead of trusting one judge.

papers.title: Bayesian control for coding agents

notes.takeaway: Makes tool-use scheduling a cost-sensitive decision instead of a fixed rule: a controller holds a belief b=P(correct) over the current candidate and, per step, chooses a cheap critic, a regeneration, or the expensive oracle verifier by comparing Q-values that subtract each action's measured cost. Costs are logged from deployment (latency, tokens, API cost), giving a slow-oracle regime (Cver=90) and a fast-oracle regime (Cver=5). Pooling 7,020 sweep points over the (prior, Cver/R) plane yields three regimes: Bayesian control wins when Cver/R is at least ~1 (verification as costly as the reward), a single public-test gate wins at moderate cost when that critic is near-oracle, and always-verify wins when verification is cheap or the prior pass rate is already high. On SWE-Bench Lite both Bayesian controllers beat always-verify while best-of-3, Self-Refine, and Reflexion underperform it.
notes.why: The routing/cost thesis made rigorous: never treat an unknown action cost as zero, record cost facts first, and let the cost-to-reward ratio pick the schedule. Fan-out and always-on verification lose precisely where verification is expensive; a cost-aware cascade that gates on cheap critics and verifies only past a posterior threshold wins there — and the always-verify pocket shows orchestration is itself a cost that can exceed its benefit.

papers.title: AgentLens: Interpretable Safety Steering via Mechanistic Subspaces for Multi-Turn Coding Agent

notes.takeaway: A white-box runtime defense for multi-turn coding agents that drive a shell in Docker. At each step it reads the last-token hidden state at one layer and runs a single linear probe to flag a harmful execution state; on a flag it steers the representation inside a sparse 10-dimensional subspace, adapting only the steering strength via an LLM judge scoring safety (0.6) and utility (0.4). It detects current-step risk at 97.32% average accuracy, predicts the next harmful command at up to 96.77% lookahead, and cuts average attack success from 85.99% to 13.36% (72.63 pp), beating RepE and self-reminder. Negative steering of the same subspace flips genuine refusals into malicious commands (100% ASR on LLaMA), confirming the direction is causal not lexical; under prompt injection the probe misfires but applying the steering direction still drops ASR 86.7%->6.7%.
notes.why: Coding agents that run a shell are an OS-level attack surface where harm accumulates across turns and injection enters through tool output, not the user instruction. This shows governance can move inside the model — step-level detection plus representation-level mitigation — but the bidirectional causal result is also a warning: the same subspace that enforces refusal can be reversed to strip alignment, and the 18.54% generation-collapse rate marks the deployment limit.

papers.title: ESAA-Conversational: An Event-Sourced Memory Layer for Continuity, Handoff, and Curation Across Heterogeneous LLM Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: Replaces lossy manual context copy-paste between agents with durable event-sourced state: visible turns are captured into an append-only log and projected into a handoff.md entry contract the next agent reads first. Motivated by long-context attention degradation, the cold agent reads compact read models plus a selective window, not the whole transcript.
notes.why: A direct instance of 'durable state beats conversational handoff' — continuity across agent sessions is reframed as an event-sourcing problem rather than a conversational one.

papers.title: To Run or Not to Run: Analyzing the Cost-Effectiveness of Code Execution in LLM-Based Program Repair

notes.takeaway: A controlled study holding the agent scaffold fixed (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) and varying only execution access across four paradigms: prohibiting test execution costs only a 1.25pp resolve-rate drop on commercial agents (not significant, p>0.05; ≈0pp for OpenCode) while saving 56–62% tokens and 48–54% wall-clock on Claude Code and removing per-repository test-environment upkeep. Agents average 8.8 runs/task (range 2–19) and apply execution indiscriminately.
notes.why: Quantifies the cost facts of a capability agents treat as free — execution carries a real, mostly-unjustified token, latency, and infrastructure bill, and should be scheduled by cost-benefit rather than run by default.

notes.takeaway: Execution benefit is concentrated, not uniform: 54–66% of commercial-agent cases resolve in a single edit, and 81–100% of *failed* cases pass the agent's own executed validation yet fail the official SWE-bench evaluation; OpenCode/Qwen2.5-Coder-32B instead over-retries with only 11% of failed cases passing self-validation.
notes.why: The agent's execution-based self-check is a miscalibrated success signal — passing self-validation is not ground truth — which is exactly the honest-baseline, calibrated-evaluation problem this branch is about.

papers.title: Agent-as-a-Router: Agentic Model Routing for Coding Tasks

notes.takeaway: Frames per-task model selection as a Context→Action→Feedback loop (a contextual bandit): the router picks a model, runs its output in a sandbox to get a verified score and the token-derived monetary cost, then memorizes that outcome for the next decision. ACRouter reaches the lowest cumulative regret (205.5) and highest AvgPerf (49.98%) on the in-distribution stream — beating DimensionBest, which holds a full dimension-level prior, by 2.48% AvgPerf — while keeping Perf/$ above always-using-the-strongest model (3.79 vs 1.29 ID; 1.18 vs 0.64 OOD).
notes.why: A concrete adaptive router that records cost facts per decision (never treating unknown cost as zero) and conditions on accumulated outcomes beats always-on use of the strongest model — the cost-and-routing pillar made measurable.

notes.takeaway: An ablation isolates the router's bottleneck as information deficit, not reasoning: handing a zero-shot LLM router per-dimension performance statistics lifts AvgPerf 15.3% (41.41→47.74) and beats the heuristic encoding the same priors. CodeRouterBench grounds every score in sandbox execution across ~10K tasks and 8 frontier LLMs and scores routers by cumulative regret against a per-task oracle rather than by self-report.
notes.why: Models the evaluation pillar: anchor on an honest baseline (the per-task oracle / cumulative regret) and verify each decision by execution instead of trusting model self-assessment.

papers.title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards

notes.takeaway: Characterizes verification signals along three axes (scalability, faithfulness, robustness) and shows no verifier achieves all three: unit tests are scalable and robust but cover a thin layer of intent, LLM judges are scalable and faithful but gameable, human review is faithful and robust but cannot scale. Adding an agentic quality judge plus trajectory-level behavior monitoring to test-driven rewards cut the hacked resolved rate across three SWE-Bench variants from 28.57% to 0.56% while raising the clean resolved rate from 40.22% to 60.53%.
notes.why: Direct evidence for this branch's stance that eval is risk reduction, not proof: no fixed reward function survives a strengthening policy, so verification has to co-evolve with the generator rather than be built once.

papers.title: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators

notes.takeaway: Makes the evaluator part of the self-improvement search: epochs run with a frozen evaluator, a challenger is promoted at an epoch boundary only if it statistically beats the incumbent on held-out ground truth, and utility records scored by the displaced evaluator are selectively erased. A co-evolved agent-as-a-judge code reviewer lifts held-out Polyglot pass rate to 71.7% against the prior SOTA's 69.9% with 1.35–1.72× fewer search tokens.
notes.why: Concrete machinery for judge calibration under optimization pressure: static verifiers saturate or get hacked, and the paper answers with per-epoch stationarity plus evaluator replacement, including an adversarial epoch that debiased a reviewer over-accepting AI-generated papers at up to 1.91× the human rate.

papers.title: Dockerless: Environment-Free Program Verifier for Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: Verifies patches without executing them: the verifier derives verification questions from the issue and reference patch, dispatches parallel read-only sub-agents (find, grep, rg) to gather repository evidence, and turns a binary verdict token's logits into a continuous score. Trained by rejection sampling on 3.7K execution-labeled issues, it beats the strongest open-source verifier by 14.3 AUC points and powers a fully environment-free SFT+RL pipeline that matches environment-based post-training (62.0/50.0/35.2 on SWE-bench Verified/Multilingual/Pro).
notes.why: Grounds this branch's execution-first maxim from the other side: where per-repository Docker environments are infeasible (private, legacy, enterprise codebases), repository-grounded agentic judgment rather than surface patch matching is what keeps the reward signal honest.

papers.title: Are Performance-Optimization Benchmarks Reliably Measuring Coding Agents?

notes.takeaway: Cross-machine replay of 740 official reference patches on four Google Cloud machine types shows the reference signal of performance benchmarks is far less stable than assumed: only 39/102 GSO, 11/140 SWE-Perf, and 411/498 SWE-fficiency tasks stay valid under their own rules in every replay, and scoring rules alone flip 9 of 28 pairwise submission comparisons, with SWE-fficiency's ten worst tasks carrying 58.5–82.8% of a submission's score weight.
notes.why: A worked example of this branch's honest-baseline demand: leaderboard aggregates conflate runtime noise, scoring-rule leverage, and task saturation. At least one public submission already beats the base code on 99.8% of replay-valid tasks, so aggregate rankings hide where the real capability gaps remain.

papers.title: Cheap Code, Costly Judgment: A Case Study on Governable Agentic Software Engineering

notes.takeaway: From a 12-week first-person case (88 contemporaneous field notes, 420 KLOC production code, 1.16 MLOC tests, lints, docs, and agent tooling) it derives 'governance conversion': agentic velocity surfaces recurring structural failure classes, and the scarce human work is not implementation-level review but recognizing which failures reveal missing governance and converting them into durable architecture and controls.
notes.why: Reframes this branch's oversight question: keeping a human near the implementation loop makes attention the throughput bottleneck, so the sustainable role is ex-post, converting observed failures into the engineering environment that constrains subsequent agent work.

papers.title: The Log Is the Agent

notes.takeaway: Recovery is replay, not handoff: any run is byte-reproducible from its log, and a fork branches at any event with the shared prefix served entirely from the content-addressed cache, so a fork of a 200-step run that changes one setting at step 150 pays only for steps 150 onward, the first 149 steps including their model calls are free. Side effects get transactional honesty rather than pretense: an external tool that mutates the world still mutates it on first execution, and only the recorded response replays deterministically; runaway reactive cascades halt against per-run budget caps on events, behavior calls, model calls, patches, recursion depth, wall-clock time, and cost.
notes.why: This branch holds that durable state beats conversational handoff, and the paper supplies the mechanism: state as a deterministic fold over an append-only log means resuming, auditing, or branching a run never depends on re-prompting or re-executing nondeterministic steps, while the side-effect caveat marks exactly where the transaction boundary sits.

notes.takeaway: Every event carries id, type, payload, actor, a caused_by pointer to the triggering event, and a timestamp, giving end-to-end lineage from a high-level goal down to the individual model call: a claim like 'Northwind Q3 revenue grew 28% YoY to $42M' names the behavior that created it (document_researcher), the event that caused it, and the specific model request event that produced it. The worked diligence run yields 671 events, 93 objects, and 76 relations via 103 model calls and 48 tool calls, and strict replay compares the live event stream against the recorded one, pinning any divergence to the first event that differs.
notes.why: This branch says transcripts are not observability; the paper operationalizes the alternative, a structured, causally-linked, replayable trace where 'why is this fact in the agent's working set' becomes a query over the log, and a green strict replay is a machine-checkable proof that intent and action still correlate.

papers.title: Exploiting LLM Agent Supply Chains via Payload-Less Skills

notes.takeaway: Semantic Compliance Hijacking (SCH) weaponizes third-party Agent Skill files without any embedded code: it injects obfuscated natural-language 'compliance guidelines' that the agent's retrieve-contextualize-execute pipeline fuses directly into the LLM system prompt as authoritative directives, and the agent then synthesizes and runs the malicious logic itself at runtime (dumping os.environ and POSTing it as 'telemetry', or exec()-ing a fetched remote byte stream). Across 600 contextualized tasks over 3 frameworks (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and 3 models, SCH hit a peak 77.67% complete-leakage rate and 67.33% RCE, yet both SkillScan (AST/regex) and LLM Guard (semantic classifiers) flagged it at 0.00%, versus 62.00-96.00% detection for SkillJect and 91.61-99.81% for DDIPE explicit-payload baselines; an 'Alignment-Security Paradox' made the most-aligned model (GPT-5.4 mini, 62.11% avg complete leakage) the most exploitable because it best maps prose directives to concrete system APIs.
notes.why: It concretely demonstrates the branch's premise that skill/tool documentation entering an agent's context is untrusted input and that the skill marketplace is an attack-surface topology: a benign-looking natural-language file propagates through the load-and-execute chain into host-privileged code execution, defeating signature-based scanning and forcing the shift to semantic intent validation and bounded autonomy (declared network endpoints and read/write paths via an ABOM contract).

papers.title: Knowledge-Based Pull Requests: A Trusted Workflow for Agent-Mediated Knowledge Collaboration

notes.takeaway: KPR treats an external collaborator's code, tests, and agent trace as a knowledge source, not a merge candidate; only a project-owned inner trusted coding agent regenerates code inside the receiving project's environment, under repository context and security policy, before anything can be merged.
notes.why: Reframes the trust boundary itself: external artifacts never cross directly into the mergeable-code path, which structurally blocks a class of attacks that traditional PR review of an external diff cannot.

notes.takeaway: A human-confirmed knowledge package (design memo, risk checklist, test plan) sits between external exploration and code generation, so project-side reviewers judge intent and evidence before any project-owned agent writes mergeable code.
notes.why: Separates two decisions traditional PRs conflate, whether knowledge should enter the project and whether an implementation should be merged, keeping humans on the judgment call rather than only on a final diff review.

papers.title: Govern the Repository, Not the Agent: Measuring Ecosystem-Level Risk in AI-Native Software

notes.takeaway: Across 930,000+ agent-authored pull requests, multilevel models show about half the variance in integration friction survives after accounting for the contribution, its author, size, and agent, and it is a repository-level property. Agent-authored contributions concentrate this repository-level friction roughly twice as much as human ones (ICC 0.30 vs 0.16).
notes.why: Direct evidence that reliability failures in agentic development are often ecosystem-level, not fixable by improving any one agent, arguing for governing and measuring at the repository level.

papers.title: Glite ARF: Verifier-Driven Research with Parallel LLM Coding Agents

notes.takeaway: Glite ARF enforces task-level worktree isolation and immutability with a corrections overlay after an incident where one agent step recomputed and corrupted 20,304 historical training rows across 38 feature sets; completed task folders can't be modified, so fixes are separate, auditable downstream tasks.
notes.why: A concrete production incident, not a hypothetical, driving the isolation and immutability design, showing what breaks when many parallel coding agents share a research repo without structural guardrails.

notes.takeaway: A materialized, git-committed 'overview/' dashboard is regenerated by deterministic aggregator scripts and is the only human-facing summary in the repo, built after stale or hand-edited tracker files misled reviewers (one reported '75 of 64' completed tasks).
notes.why: A concrete answer to 'transcripts are not observability': a structured, always-regenerated artifact rather than an agent-written summary or a manually maintained log.

papers.title: NOVA: A Verification-Aware Agent Harness for Architecture Evolution in Industrial Recommender Systems

notes.takeaway: NOVA's verification cascade checks architecture semantics before expensive training or deployment, catching runnable-but-structurally-invalid candidates that pass unit tests but violate recommender-specific invariants like sequence masking; failed-verification diagnostics become reusable 'forbidden directions' that shape later search.
notes.why: A concrete example of test-passing code that is still wrong at the architecture-semantics level, the exact silent-failure class this branch tracks, plus a mechanism for learning from verification failures rather than only gating them.

notes.takeaway: Deployed in a production advertising system serving over a billion users, NOVA is evaluated against human-expert loops, AutoML, and generic coding-agent baselines with both offline metrics and live online A/B testing, improving GMV on three pCVR objectives by 1.25-2.02% while cutting prediction bias 37.3-66.7%.
notes.why: Grounds evaluation in actual production execution and online A/B results rather than only offline benchmark scores or LLM-judge ratings.

notes.takeaway: An L1-L4 task-level control scheme routes higher-risk architecture changes to a human-in-the-loop 'Copilot' mode rather than full autonomy, matching automation level to task complexity and risk.
notes.why: A concrete risk-tiered autonomy design rather than a binary autonomous-or-not choice, for the human-oversight branch.

papers.title: TrajAudit: Automated Failure Diagnosis for Agentic Coding Systems

notes.takeaway: RootSE distills 93 real repository-level agent failures (over 4,500 execution steps) into a diagnosis benchmark whose target is the earliest decisive error step - the single early mistake, such as a misread requirement or flawed plan, whose cumulative consequence is the eventual system failure.
notes.why: This branch tracks the failure taxonomy you need before scaling agent fan-out; RootSE is a concrete, complexity-graded catalog of how repo-level coding agents actually fail and where the decisive error first enters the trajectory.

notes.takeaway: TrajAudit treats the raw trajectory as mostly noise (tool observations are over 70% of content) and replaces passive whole-trace ingestion with an investigator agent that folds observations down to failure-relevant fragments and retrieves detail on demand, lifting localization accuracy by over 24.4 points while cutting token use at least 18%.
notes.why: The branch's claim is that a transcript is not observability; TrajAudit is a worked case where structured, on-demand retrieval over the trace correlates the decisive action with the failure far better than feeding the model the entire log, which drops prior methods below 40% on long trajectories.

papers.title: TTHE: Test-Time Harness Evolution

notes.takeaway: TTHE selects an improved agent harness during evaluation with no gold labels, committing candidate programs from execution-derived proxy signals via an agentic judge; its own trace audits attribute the remaining errors to that judge committing a plausible-but-wrong harness under imperfect proxies, and gains are non-monotonic in search budget.
notes.why: This branch grounds evaluation in execution and calibrated judges; TTHE is a direct study of the failure mode, naming execution-proxy reliability and judge calibration as the central bottleneck when execution stands in for an honest label.

papers.title: Tool-Making and Self-Evolving LLM Agents in Low-Latency Systems

notes.takeaway: The runtime is a cascade - a cheap compiled tool per SOP node first, code generation only when a tool is missing or fails - and the paper records concrete cost facts from production: p50 latency down 42%, a further 62% from the resulting direct-call architecture, and end-to-end error rate down up to 53% from suppressed run-to-run variance.
notes.why: The branch holds that cascades beat always-on regeneration and that you record cost facts before optimizing routing; this is a deployed fulfillment-center instance with measured latency and error deltas rather than a treat-unknown-cost-as-zero estimate.

papers.title: 3100 Opinions on Code Review in an AI World: Building Causal Theory from Practitioner Discourse

notes.takeaway: Synthesizing 3,100 coded practitioner documents into a 26-construct, 67-relationship causal model, the paper's organizing claim is that code review is the control point through which a coding agent's effect on software is decided, and AI does not fix the sign of that effect - human expertise and how the team structures review set it; its observational study finds 40.1% of agent-authored PRs examined only by the developer who invoked the agent versus 21.5% of human PRs.
notes.why: This branch is about keeping humans on the reasoning chain; the paper supplies the theory of why that matters for agent-authored code - review is the human control point where the agent's effect is decided, and delegating it away (self-review, or no review) is where oversight quietly erodes.

papers.title: From Prompts to Contracts: Harness Engineering for Auditable Enterprise LLM Agents

notes.takeaway: The harness makes the assembly trace a checked artifact rather than a byproduct: every reader-facing answer records how it was built from bounded sources, trace completeness is one of the enforced contracts, and internal-trace or identifier leakage is caught before it reaches the reader. In the adversarial ablation, prompt-only leaked internal identifiers or trace records on all 15 leak-bait runs, each of which the harness blocked.
notes.why: This branch holds that transcripts are not observability; the paper operationalizes a structured trace that ties each visible claim back to the sources and routing that produced it, and treats trace leakage as a governed failure the system detects, not an accident.

notes.takeaway: Assurance is grounded in executable validators plus honest controls. A fault-injection negative control confirms the validators actually flag deliberately broken source, routing, trace, answer, and leakage contracts, and an enforcement-layer ablation shows the code-owned gate is load-bearing rather than reproducible by prompting. A bolt-on external guardrail blocks the same violations but over-refuses, with 4 false refusals and 28 of 30 adversarial runs blocked, dropping utility to 88/120 where the harness preserves 120/120 by falling back to a deterministic composer.
notes.why: This branch treats evaluation as risk reduction against an honest baseline; the paper measures the enforcement layer against both a negative control and a competing guardrail, separating whether a violation is blocked from whether utility survives, which is the tradeoff assurance work has to report.

notes.takeaway: Governance holds only because it is code-owned, not prompted. With the model fixed and only the enforcement layer varied, prompt instructions alone let recommendation-language and internal-trace-leakage violations reach the reader on all 30 adversarial runs, every one of which the harness blocked; only source-backed claims are allowed to enter runtime context in the first place. Across 270 composition-boundary runs under three substituted models the contracts held, with failures confined to the model-composed side and recorded.
notes.why: This branch treats output hygiene and untrusted retrieved content as an enforced surface; the paper shows source boundaries and output-hygiene contracts survive model substitution only when enforcement lives in code, which is the governance property the branch tracks.

papers.title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?

notes.takeaway: Evaluation is grounded in execution with an honest floor built into the metric. Each of 263 tasks is a pair sharing one sandbox that differs by a single controlled perturbation, so passing both the should-act and should-abstain side (Paired Accuracy, the primary metric) caps any always-act or always-refuse policy at 50%. Scoring pairs a deterministic commit-check on the tool-call trace with an LLM judge on the terminal response, catching failures either signal alone misses, and a Conditioned Abstention Rate restricts the abstain score to pairs whose act side already passed, isolating restraint from baseline task skill. AbstainGen regenerates fresh task instances on demand, validated by deterministic DAG replay and cross-family LLM critics, to resist contamination.
notes.why: This branch holds that evaluation should be grounded in execution against an honest baseline with calibrated judges. AgentAbstain builds the honest baseline into the metric itself, grades pass or fail on the executable commit trace rather than the wording of the reply, and separates restraint from task competence, which is how the branch wants abstention assurance reported.

notes.takeaway: The paper gives an agent-native failure taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios, organized by when a trigger becomes observable (pre-execution reasoning vs. runtime discovery) and where it resides (query, environment state, or tools). Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 harnesses the best agent, Gemini 3.1 Pro, reaches only 59.5% Paired Accuracy and 13 of 17 stay below 50%, and abstention capability tracks largely independently of general task-solving skill. The signature failure is post-hoc abstention: an agent commits an irreversible action, such as cancelling a flight before checking rebooking availability, then verbally acknowledges the problem, leaving unrecoverable side effects.
notes.why: This branch is about knowing the failure taxonomy before scaling. AgentAbstain names the failure modes that appear once agents can commit irreversible actions on a user's behalf, and shows model scale alone does not close the gap, so restraint has to be engineered rather than assumed as capability grows.

papers.title: Learning Latency-Aware Orchestration for Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Cost and latency are not the same objective over an execution graph: cost accumulates additively over every operator, while latency is the maximum over source-to-sink paths, so two graphs with equal accuracy and equal cost can differ substantially in wall-clock time. LAMaS schedules against that distinction, reporting critical-path output tokens (CP Tokens) alongside wall-clock latency as a structural indicator of bottleneck workload; on GSM8K it holds 93.65% accuracy at 622 CP Tokens and 7.71e-4 USD per query against MaAS at 93.36%, 2501 CP Tokens and 31.52e-4 USD. The inference-time controller supplies the run-time trim a training-time graph cannot: removing it costs 16.5-21.1% latency and 16.0-25.2% cost while accuracy moves under 0.38 points.
notes.why: This branch holds that cost facts should be recorded before routing is optimized and that unknown cost is never zero. The paper extends that to scheduling: measuring total cost alone leaves the latency bottleneck unattributed, because a uniform penalty gives the same gradient to operators that cannot affect wall-clock time as to the ones that set it. Removing the latency objective entirely leaves accuracy within 0.25 points but inflates latency 24-70% and cost 19-35%, so the structure-aware objective is buying real deployment margin rather than trading accuracy away.

papers.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents

notes.takeaway: On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.4 mini under matched feedback and inference budgets, automatic harness evolution does not consistently beat simple test-time scaling: without unit tests it averages 67.4 pass@1 versus 72.3 for parallel sampling (and drops GPT-5.4 from 75.3 to 69.7), and a harness evolved on 45 training tasks transfers to 34 held-out tasks for only +0.6 pass@1 on average.
notes.why: Assurance has to be grounded in an honest baseline: because harness evolution is itself a search procedure evaluated on the same benchmark it searches over, its reported gains are largely repeated-sampling gains and overfit the search set, a direct warning about how agent-improvement methods are measured before they are trusted in production.

papers.title: Cache-Aware Prompt Compression: A Two-Tier Cost Model for LLM API Caching

notes.takeaway: Measures Anthropic's production prompt cache and finds a two-tier architecture with a sharp threshold near 3,500 tokens (hit rate plateaus at 0.83 below it, reaches ~1.0 above), then derives a cost model showing that query-aware compression, which rewrites the prefix every call and so voids the cache, is strictly dominated: cache-aware query-agnostic compression (CAPC) with a tier-preserving ratio bound is cheapest in 16 of 16 LongBench-v2 configurations, with mean savings of 49% over cache-only and 90% over vanilla.
notes.why: A direct instance of recording cost facts before optimizing: the compression literature's implicit assumption of a perfect cache hit rate misstates the real cost landscape, and on tau-bench retail the standard query-aware method costs 40.1% more than doing nothing at identical task reward, so the measured cost model, not the compression ratio, decides the routing choice.

papers.title: Where Does Agent Reliability Come From? A Cross-Benchmark Decomposition of Verification Loops, Specialist Models, and Scaffolding in a Production Enterprise Agent

notes.takeaway: Decomposes a production enterprise agent's uplift over its bare base model (+11.0 pp on SpreadsheetBench Verified, +7-10 pp on BullshitBench v2, ~+15 pp on GAIA validation) by architectural layer: scaffolding and prompting account for +9.5 of the +11.0 pp on SpreadsheetBench, while the verification loop's isolated contribution is +1.5 pp (6 rescued tasks) - small but concentrated at the top of the score distribution, where every competitive system has already exhausted scaffolding gains. A specialist-swap ablation shows the loop's value rides on observer independence: moving observe/compare from the small trained verifier back onto the frontier model that generated the artifact cuts SpreadsheetBench rescues from 6 tasks to 2 and drops BullshitBench correct rejection 4-5 pp.
notes.why: Answers the branch's question with measurement instead of architecture faith: most of a verification-loop system's reliability comes from unglamorous structure (prompting, planner-executor splits, routing), so teams should invest there first - but the tail of a reliability SLA still needs the checkpoint, staffed by an observer that did not write the artifact.

notes.takeaway: A vendor evaluation that does the honesty work: it retires the company's own earlier 77.6% GAIA figure after re-grading all 803 stored trajectories with the official scorer (the old number mixed best-of-k and pass@1 across tiers; clean pass@1 is 75.2%), runs a scripted retrieval-contamination audit that brackets the GAIA result at [70.9%, 75.2%], n-gram-scans 30,104 production messages against 365 evaluation items to audit specialist training contamination (4 matches, all from internal test accounts excluded from training), reports Wilson CIs throughout, and states which cross-system comparisons are statistically unresolvable, with measured run-to-run sensitivity of ~3 pp.
notes.why: A working template for the branch's honest-baseline demand: self-correcting a published headline, shipping contamination-audit scripts, and declaring resolvability limits are what separate evaluation-as-risk-reduction from leaderboard marketing - especially inside a vendor's evaluation of its own system.

notes.takeaway: Per-step verification is affordable because loop stages run on 0.5-4B post-trained specialists (Qwen3 bases distilled from a frontier teacher, 4-bit quantized) serving at roughly 0.02-0.1x frontier cost; on GAIA, per-step routing by the ~0.5B Route-XS specialist is credited ~4 pp of accuracy at net-negative cost, because cheap steps route to small models and fund extended reasoning on hard ones.
notes.why: Concrete cost facts for the branch's cascade thesis: small specialists observing every step while the frontier model only executes and fixes is what turns 'verify everything' from a luxury into the economical default.

papers.title: DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making

notes.takeaway: Replaying 150 fixed cases across 10 models and 3 tool-using financial tasks (8,127 episodes, 1,338 case groups) separates Decision Agreement Rate from Trajectory Agreement Rate, and the two come apart: Claude Sonnet 4 agrees on compliance decisions 94.7% of the time but matches its own tool-call sequence only 76.7% of the time, an 18-point gap. Chance correction widens the picture - the three trajectory divergers fall from headline DAR of 0.86-0.95 to Fleiss' kappa of 0.53-0.56 once each model's own marginal label preferences are subtracted, and Claude Sonnet on DataOps reaches kappa = 0.054 at DAR = 0.947. Across the 10 model rows, modal-decision accuracy is not detectably correlated with DAR (rho = 0.115, permutation p = 0.763) or with the DAR-TAR gap (rho = -0.048, p = 0.919).
notes.why: An evaluation that presents each input once and records a single answer cannot see this axis at all; the paper's phrase is that within-model consistency is invisible to between-model benchmarks by design. The instruction it hands benchmark users is concrete: report conventional accuracy and behavioral-stability metrics side by side, because in this corpus neither substitutes for the other. It also shows what a stability number alone would hide in the other direction - Qwen 3.5 scores DAR = 1.000 while averaging 48% accuracy, consistently wrong.

notes.takeaway: All three divergence channels are chosen so they require no access to hidden reasoning text: tool-call sequence, evidence-contact set scored as mean pairwise Jaccard distance over consulted tool outputs or output hashes, and decision concentration measured by normalized entropy across cases within a task. On DataOps exception handling 54.3% of evidence contacts differ across runs despite unanimous decisions. Each run records the final decision, the tool-call sequence, tool output hashes and runtime metadata, and can be packaged as an audit bundle with a SHA-256 hash chain over episode records plus an Ed25519 certificate for third-party verification. Metrics are computed only on channels actually present, with a channel-availability matrix reported alongside results - Granite 3.3 and Mistral 7B emit decisions at 0.00 tool calls per run, leaving no trajectory or evidence channel to measure.
notes.why: It draws the line between a transcript and a trace: what makes the instability measurable is the structured execution record - sequences, output hashes, an explicit availability matrix - not the model's narration of itself. The paper holds that line on its own naming, calling the phenomenon trajectory divergence rather than reasoning divergence because rationale-text coverage in the corpus is 0%. The disclosed protocol deviation (the Anthropic runner omitted an explicit temperature, so Claude episodes ran at provider default) is handled the same way: recorded in the sampling metadata and reported rather than quietly re-collected.

papers.title: IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests

notes.takeaway: Six seed issues from SymPy and requests fan out into 696 adversarial artifacts - four attack categories (installing a disguised PyPI package, planting a hidden executable validation hook that phones an attacker endpoint, poisoning .cursorrules or CLAUDE.md so the agent stops asking for terminal confirmation, and spawning 10,000 worker threads), crossed with six delivery vectors and per-vector perturbations - executed across 6 agent-model configurations for 4,176 runs. 66.5% penetrate both agent- and LLM-level guardrails. Delivery vector is the dominant factor: payloads in ordinary text artifacts (issue bodies, PDFs) succeed in 72.2% of runs against 16.7% when confined to image alt-text, while cross-lingual translation and visual obfuscation show negligible effect. Of 1,400 resisted runs, 82.9% are blocked by the model explicitly refusing and 17.1% by the model classifying the source as untrusted metadata. Spotlighting-style boundary markers failed to stop payload execution.
notes.why: It puts numbers on treating retrieved content as untrusted, and locates the control where operators usually assume it is not: resistance is almost entirely model-level, so a harness relying on its agent framework as the safety layer is relying on a layer that contributed close to nothing here. The alt-text gap points at the defense that did work - the agent judging a low-authority source as data rather than instruction - which is a provenance property of the ingestion path, not payload detection. The configuration-poisoning category is the sharpest case for anyone running an agent under a rules file: the attack's whole objective is to get the agent to rewrite its own confirmation policy, turning the guardrail into part of the attack surface.

papers.title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control

notes.takeaway: Treats every agent-emitted lifecycle claim (reviewed, tested, done, ready-to-merge) as inadmissible until fresh, tracked-source-state-bound evidence satisfies a gate. In a 9,240-cell powered ablation, the pre-registered contrast between the gated loop and a compute-budgeted naive loop cut visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31/1,800 injected cells to 2/1,800 (+1.6pp not-amplified, 95% CI [0.8, 2.5]); a near-compute contrast (14/1,800 vs 2/1,800) shows the gain tracks enforcing the review signal as a hard gate, not just adding a reviewer.
notes.why: A measured entry in the false-DONE failure taxonomy this branch tracks: it names the exact mechanism (self-report vs. gate-admissible evidence) that turns a green pipeline into a false completeness claim, and gives real numbers for how much a lifecycle gate closes that gap versus a naive loop.

notes.takeaway: Evaluates the control layer itself through mechanism tests (10/10 loop scenarios, zero false-done), the powered ablation above, and an operated self-application corpus (565 stories, 1,007 review findings, 94.8% resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit) rather than narrative claims of correctness.
notes.why: Grounds evaluation in execution exactly as this branch asks: it does not trust the agent's own account of being done, it checks whether the evidence supporting that account is fresh, tamper-resistant (18 tamper classes rejected, zero false accepts), and bound to the tracked source state.

papers.title: CAVA: Canonical Action Verification and Attestation for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems

notes.takeaway: Converts heterogeneous runtime records (local coding hooks, SDK tools, browser automation, MCP calls, CI/CD API requests, workflow engines) into a canonical, versioned, hashable, receipt-bearing action object, so an independent verifier can later reproduce what action was actually approved and executed.
notes.why: A direct instance of 'transcripts are not observability': raw runtime logs of the same action differ by runtime, so this branch's replayable-trace requirement needs exactly the stable, cross-runtime action identity CAVA formalizes.

notes.takeaway: A 96-seed, 384-variant benchmark shows raw-text and first-token approval binding are defeated by wrappers (env, sudo, bash -c, aliases, SDK indirection), while canonical fingerprinting resists wrapper bypass and approval drift; ablating the canonical fingerprint is the single most damaging removal tested, collapsing the retained score to 0.00 since there is no longer a stable object for approval to bind to.
notes.why: Puts numbers on 'topology is an attack surface': it shows concretely how an equivalent rewrite of the same action can bypass a policy bound to raw text or a first token, and measures how much a canonical action fingerprint closes that gap.

papers.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability? Protocol Validity in the Age of Agentic AI

notes.takeaway: An audit of 2,385 retained task-to-score traces across 15 agent benchmarks finds a supported score-relevant protocol finding in 67.0% of Frontier Science traces (331/494) and 66.7% of AutoLab tasks (24/36), while eleven other cohorts sit at or below 21.7% and five contain none. Where a defensible comparison score exists, the measured inflation G = S_exploit - S_intended runs 0.447 to 1.00: 1.00 for a WildClawBench empty submission that received full credit, 0.859 and 0.835 for EdgeBench evaluation-pipeline and interaction-feedback loopholes, 0.621 for a causal-discovery generator that emitted variables in topological order, and 0.447 for Frontier Science once answer access is removed. The audit itself is scored rather than asserted: 0.94 precision and 0.76 recall (F1 0.84) against 53 hand-labeled traces, and it holds negative controls non-positive when an agent reads a held-out file but does not use it in the submission.
notes.why: This branch asks for evaluation grounded in execution against an honest baseline. The paper locates the failure one level below the metric: the protocol P = {environment, information flow, scoring, verification} can make a shortcut sufficient for success without changing the nominal task, so a score is evidence of capability only when an audit establishes the full Expose -> Exploit -> Mislead chain. It also supplies the discipline this branch needs in practice - exposure, use, and awarded credit are separate claims requiring separate evidence, and a suspicious action with no effect on the score is not a finding.

papers.title: When Do Agent Loops Mistake Stagnation for Progress? Self-Evaluation Bias and Externally Grounded Verification in Long-Running Autonomous LLM Agent Loops

notes.takeaway: The testbed holds the agent and its tool surface fixed and varies only what the evaluator gating the loop can see, so the comparison isolates evaluator grounding rather than evaluator quality. Three arms sit behind one interface: in-band-self, which accepts a cycle if the agent edited files and stated a rationale; the strongest in-band judge, which reads the full artifact text, the change diff and its own verdict history; and an out-of-band evaluator that reads a world-state oracle with its own tools. Across 54 cycles the agent claimed improvement every time while 56% of those cycles had an oracle-measured delta of zero or below, so in-band-self degenerated into accept-all and eroded the best deployed state it had reached by 19% through later regressions. The strong in-band judge did not close the gap: it accepted cycles of which 44% were real-world regressions and rejected 38% of real improvements, rejecting the preregistered hypothesis that a better judge suffices. Two controls pin the mechanism down. On a boundary task whose success specification is verifiable from the artifact itself, the same judge's mirage rate fell to zero and the gap to out-of-band closed within the registered threshold. In a sign-only variant that strips the oracle numbers and returns just the accept/reject verdict, real-world output held up (mean 110.0 against 113.0 for full feedback), so the benefit comes from where the gate is grounded, not from the richness of its feedback.
notes.why: This branch asks for evaluation grounded in execution against an honest baseline, and for LLM judges to be calibrated rather than trusted. The paper supplies the calibration numbers directly as conditional acceptance rates, and then shows that calibrating harder is the wrong lever: when the success signal lives outside the transcript, no amount of judge strength recovers it, because the evidence is not in the channel the judge reads. It also draws the boundary where in-band evaluation is legitimate, which is the useful engineering line rather than a blanket verdict on LLM-as-judge.

notes.takeaway: The paper names the failure mode, the progress mirage, and defines it as a measurable rate rather than an anecdote: the fraction of evaluator-accepted cycles whose oracle-measured delta is zero or below. The definition was deliberately widened from the preregistered wording of exactly zero, because a delta of zero excludes the worse error of accepting an outright regression. Alongside it the paper reports a wasted-cycle ratio, acceptance rates conditioned separately on non-positive and positive deltas, and time-to-first-positive with right-censoring recorded, all computed mechanically from raw cycle logs with no human discretion.
