Four thin services hold the fleet together: a tool gateway gating what a container may call, a solution registry recording what was deployed and by whom, a skill library resolved across built-in, shared-platform and project tiers (baked into the image at build time by default, or re-fetched per run with its own scoped repo token for anything named under live_skills), and a run-trigger endpoint. Shipping is forking a reference repo, editing an instructions file and a config file, and pushing.
notes.why: The branch's position is to choose topology deliberately and keep roles in configuration rather than code. This paper pushes that to its limit: the same binary in every position, with the difference between a cron job, a chat backend, and a developer terminal reduced to two text files and an identity, so auditing N solutions becomes reading N version-controlled instruction files. It is an architecture proposal informed by European enterprise engagements and implemented against Azure, not a measured comparison; the paper runs no benchmark and names microcc as its reference implementation.

papers.title: SABER: Benchmarking Operational Safety of LLM Coding Agents in Stateful Project Workspaces

notes.takeaway: SABER judges completed runs, not model responses. Each of 716 tasks initializes a Docker-sandboxed workspace with source, configuration and git history, records the shell trajectory, tool calls, outputs and state deltas, and adjudicates with a rule-based checker (harmful command patterns, global safety properties) plus an LLM judge. The primary metric, harmful safety-violation rate, is computed over effective runs with incapable runs excluded, so a model gains nothing by failing to act; incapability rate and justified safe-refusal rate are reported separately. That separation carries the result: DeepSeek-V3 looks safe largely because it cannot find a path (IR 26.1%), while Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 hold the lowest violation rates (54.7%, 63.9%) and the highest late-refusal rates (9.0%, 7.4%) because they attempt more and recognize risk after harm. Nine existing safety benchmarks are run alongside and disagree with each other and with SABER.
notes.why: This branch's line is to ground evaluation in execution against an honest baseline and to treat eval as risk reduction rather than proof. SABER is the concrete version for agent safety: it closes the do-nothing loophole by excluding incapability from the denominator, and it states its own limits plainly, measuring the model's safety reasoning under one shared ReAct-style harness rather than any vendor's confirmation policies, rollback, or filters, with mock networking and Docker sandboxes that do not reproduce cloud IAM, multi-user permissions, or long-running services.

notes.takeaway: The attack surface is the whole readable workspace, not the prompt. SABER separates three causal origins: 289 tasks hide malicious instructions in project artifacts such as build metadata or dependency manifests (70.1% HSR, with 23.0% of effective runs showing multi-step compositional harm), 186 tasks are entirely benign requests where an unsafe shortcut is available (68.3% HSR with no adversary present at all), and 241 tasks put safety-relevant warnings in the workspace (82.5% HSR, the worst split). Cause labels put operational misunderstanding at 47.7% of harmful runs, ahead of injection-following at 25.4% and harmful-operation compliance at 25.1%. Capability does not buy safety: DeepSeek-V3.2 exceeds V3 at 79.6% vs 72.4% HSR while being less incapable, and Qwen3.5 moves only from 78.6% at 9B to 73.4% at 397B.
notes.why: The branch holds that tool and retrieval output is untrusted and that harm propagates. SABER extends both: the untrusted content sits in the project's own build files and git history rather than in a prompt or tool response, and the largest harm category is not injection at all but an agent choosing a destructive path toward a legitimate goal, such as chmod -R 777 to clear a permission error or a database reset that is routine in development and catastrophic in production. Refusal hardening addresses neither, and warnings already present in the workspace do not become execution constraints.

papers.title: From SQL Generation to Tool Selection: A Domain-Oriented Pattern for MCP Servers

notes.takeaway: The paper's routing claim is that the model tier a workload needs is set by the tool interface, not by the workload. Replacing an MCP server's generic execute_sql tool with five domain-aligned tools whose parameterized SQL is pre-authored server-side turns the model's job from open-ended SQL synthesis into intent classification and slot filling — the authors call the effect Model Demotion. Measured over 609 completed cells (four local 3B-8B models, seventeen Sakila tasks, temperature 0, three repetitions), the domain pack scores 0.939 pooled mean against 0.666 for raw SQL, and the smallest model, llama3.2:3b, goes from 0.583 to 0.929, matching or beating every larger configuration. Cost is reported per correct answer rather than per call: 2,723 tokens and 3.4 s for the 3B model with domain tools against 31,476 tokens and 49.5 s for the same model on raw SQL, an 11.6x reduction, with 2.0x to 3.7x reductions for the larger models. Mean per-cell tokens barely move (3,056 vs 3,953), so the entire gain is in the correct-answer denominator. A third arm matters as much as the first two: a deliberately shallow table-oriented pack pools at 0.605, below raw SQL, so a tool layer without domain design can be worse than none.
notes.why: This branch's position is that cost facts should be recorded before routing is optimized and that unknown cost must never be treated as zero. The paper is a clean instance of both. It reports cost per correct answer, which is the metric that inverts the naive reading — per-call tokens are flat while the economics change by an order of magnitude — and it locates the lever in the server-side abstraction rather than in a cascade or a router. That is a different move than the usual cascade argument: instead of choosing a cheaper model for easy requests, it makes the requests structurally easier so a cheap model suffices, with the exceptional remainder routed to a human who commits a new YAML/SQL definition and permanently absorbs the case into the deterministic set. The failure-mode argument is the reliability half: synthesis failures are open-ended (wrong joins, invalid syntax, hallucinated columns) while selection failures are bounded (wrong tool, missing parameter) and therefore detectable and loggable.

papers.title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion

notes.takeaway: FrontierChallenge curates 300 end-to-end scientific workflows and releases 97 of them across quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment, then runs twelve frontier models across three scaffolds (Codex, Claude Code, Frontier Agent). Pass Rate, the fraction of tasks satisfying the complete deliverable contract, ranged from 3.1% to 20.6% while Avg. Score ranged from 67.5 to 87.9; the two best configurations, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex and Grok 4.6 with Claude Code, each completed 20 of 97 tasks. The divergence is worst where partial credit looks best: analytical chemistry reached an Avg. Score of 87.6 with a top Pass Rate of 4%, and electrochemistry/environment reached 94.9 with a Pass Rate of 0% for every configuration. Two behavioral signals fail as completion evidence. Of 849 non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 641 (75.5%) ended with a final message claiming completion and only 13 (1.5%) said work was still running. Raw tool errors were more common in passing runs than failing ones (94.2% versus 80.7% of trajectories; medians 5.6 versus 4.4 errors per 100 tool results), so an error count identifies neither the contract breach nor the successful run.
notes.why: The failure taxonomy this branch asks you to know before scaling is here stated in terms a deployment can act on: a high average score, a confident final message, and a clean error log are each independently uninformative about whether the work was actually delivered. Completion has to be checked against the artifact bundle, by something other than the agent that produced it.

notes.takeaway: Evaluation is per-task and executable. Each of the 97 tasks ships a Grader that checks required files, numerical results, formats, figures, code execution, and cross-artifact consistency, with rubric-defined semantic criteria delegated to a GPT-5.6 Sol judge run three times and averaged. Because averaging three judge passes can pull a fully compliant submission slightly under 100, the full-completion indicator is set at a score of at least 99.9; the authors are explicit that this absorbs numerical variation and relaxes no rubric requirement. Avg. Score is reported only as a descriptive suite-level aggregate and is not treated as a calibrated cross-task scale, since the rubrics are heterogeneous. Failure signatures are read the same way: judge-assessed artifact shortfalls appeared in 97% of non-passing materials-characterization submissions and 43% of quantum-chemistry ones, while deterministic Grader diagnostics were more common in life science (50%) and quantum chemistry (40%), and the authors decline to read those contrasts as intrinsic domain difficulty.
notes.why: This is what grounding evaluation in execution costs and buys. The judge is confined to rubric criteria inside a deterministic Grader rather than scoring the submission end to end, the aggregate metric is labelled descriptive rather than comparable, and the pass threshold is derived from the judge's own measured variance instead of being assumed.

papers.title: StarHarness: Evolving Harnesses with Stratified Search for Enterprise Environments

notes.takeaway: StarHarness holds model weights fixed and searches the executable scaffold around them: prompt and task framing, tool definitions and schemas, argument preprocessing, skills, MCP providers, subagent structure, context management, verification, and finish logic. The evolution pool is stratified by baseline failure mode (wrong_tool, context_loss, missing_evidence, premature_conclusion), baseline score, and verifier pass rate, then split into proposer-visible search tasks and proposer-hidden selection tasks with matched distributions, leaving a holdout that never touches proposal or acceptance. Twenty-one patches were accepted in total: 4 on ITBench, 12 on EnterpriseOps-Gym, 5 on AutomationBench. ITBench went from 40.0% to 75.0% with false positives falling from 0.79 to 0.33 and true positives rising from 0.45 to 0.78; EnterpriseOps-Gym went from 23.3% to 43.7% with verifier pass rate rising from 34.5% to 72.8%; AutomationBench went from 57.1% to 83.2% with tasks incurring guardrail violations falling from 20 to 4 and zero-score tasks from 24 to 6. Held-out gains were +31.7, +15.1, and +29.3 percentage points. The frozen harness, evolved once with GPT-5.4, improved every transferred model across GPT and Qwen families without re-evolution, by +10.7 to +46.3 points. The accepted edits fall into three kinds: interface repair (stripping null and placeholder arguments before they reach a strict MCP server, preserving compound schemas), environment conventions made explicit (coupled priority and impact updates, preserving relationship fields, anchoring relative dates to the sandbox clock), and operational knowledge that compresses search (a forensics overview ranking candidate upstream causes, deterministic date and finance calculators).
notes.why: The failure being repaired is model-environment mismatch, not model capability, and it is invisible to anyone who only measures the model. The evaluation design is the part worth copying: proposer-hidden selection plus an untouched holdout separates search performance from generalization, which the authors note a comparable system did not do when it searched and reported on the same benchmark.

notes.takeaway: The cost numbers move with the scores rather than against them. Estimated GPT-5.4 inference cost per task fell 17% on ITBench ($3.26 to $2.70), 53% on EnterpriseOps-Gym ($1.23 to $0.58), and 29% on AutomationBench ($0.14 to $0.10), because the evolved harness shortened trajectories: EnterpriseOps-Gym turns fell from 18.12 to 9.87 and tool calls from 29.53 to 16.83, ITBench turns from 25.2 to 22.1 on comparable evidence inspection, AutomationBench turns from 16.35 to 11.98. The transfer table prices the alternative to buying a bigger model: Qwen3.5-27B on the evolved ITBench harness scores 70.0% against 40.0% for GPT-5.4 on the default one, and GPT-5.4-mini reaches 79.4% against the same 40.0% baseline. Guardrails keep this from being benchmark fitting; candidates may not branch on task IDs, embed verifier content in prompts, or reach ground-truth tables, and a candidate failing scope, import, or smoke checks is reverted before any selection run.
notes.why: This branch's rule is to record cost facts before optimizing routing. StarHarness records them per task alongside score, and the resulting fact inverts the usual routing move: a 27B model on an environment-adapted harness beat a frontier model on a default one, and cost per task fell rather than rising to pay for the gain.

papers.title: ToolRobustBench: Stage-Wise Perturbation Evaluation and Failure Diagnosis for Tool-Calling Agents

notes.takeaway: Clean tool-calling accuracy hides almost all of the risk. Across 7 models, 16 sampled deterministic local tools, 4 perturbation families, 14 subtypes, and 15,456 single-family records, mean clean success is 0.979 with three models at 1.000, while overall robustness under perturbation runs 0.664 to 0.766. The damage is not spread evenly across the pipeline: averaged over models, tool-interface perturbation costs least at 0.918, then user-intent at 0.773 and runtime-environment at 0.688, while tool-output/observation perturbation collapses to 0.455 with no model above 0.60. The hardest single subtype is C2 return-evidence loss at 0.142, and it is not an artifact of unsolvable tasks: 34.0% of C2 instances are solved by at least one model, and a human annotator judged the clean answer recoverable from the perturbed return in 68.3% of an audited 60. Combined stress is worse than the worst of its parts. Across five mixed-family pairs, mean success is 0.448 at medium severity against 0.621 for the weaker isolated constituent and 0.754 for the mean of both, and 0.200 against 0.292 and 0.507 at heavy severity, so composite difficulty cannot be approximated by taking the minimum of two single-axis scores.
notes.why: This branch asks for the failure taxonomy before you scale. The taxonomy here says the fragile stage is not tool selection but interpreting what a tool returned, which is exactly the stage a clean benchmark never exercises, and that stacking two independently survivable perturbations produces a drop neither one predicts.

notes.takeaway: Attribution is deterministic and uses no LLM judge. The scorer derives an observed error label through a fixed priority order (call presence, structured-format validity, tool-name resolution, canonical-tool match, required-argument presence, argument-value match, execution success), then backtracks to the earliest upstream stage compatible with the perturbation family, flagging a boundary violation only when the attributed source falls outside both the expected and allowed-spillover sets. Cascade rates separate the families sharply: runtime-environment 0.638, tool-interface 0.352, tool-output/observation 0.003, with runtime boundary violations at 0.006. The attribution is validated counterfactually rather than asserted: repairing the attributed primary stage would recover 71 of 98 failed instances, split 100% for single-fault cases, 82.1% for cascade cases, and 0% for multi-fault cases. Two targeted interventions then show the labels are prescriptive. Chain-of-thought instructions aimed at argument binding left gpt-5.4-mini at 21/30 on user-intent perturbations, because those failures were rooted in tool selection; supplying explicit aliases beside perturbed tool names took the same model from 21/30 to 30/30.
notes.why: An aggregate success rate tells you a system is failing but not which fix to buy. This is the mechanism that closes that gap, and unusually it reports the negative intervention alongside the positive one, which is what makes the diagnostic labels credible as causes rather than tags.

papers.title: Candidate supply and answer selection shape the value of LLM judging in multi-agent systems

notes.takeaway: A judge is calibrated against the pool it will actually see. Ranking reliability here is measured as rank AUC, the probability a randomly chosen correct candidate is ordered above an incorrect one from the same pool, and it varies with task, candidate generator, inference setting, and how rare correct answers are: below chance at the lowest correct-answer availability, rising to a half-rise midpoint of 14.7% in the primary four-benchmark setting, 28.6% and 36.9% on HLE multiple-choice and open-answer questions. Two generator configurations with the same mean rank AUC of 0.8493 behave completely differently as availability changes (R-squared 0.022 versus 0.928), so a headline judge score does not transfer across generators. Above-chance ranking also does not automatically become system accuracy: on 81,390 frozen pools, using the judge signal beat majority voting by 6 to 8 points where correct candidates were present but outnumbered, and lost 3.22 points where correct candidates already dominated.
notes.why: This branch says calibrate LLM judges and treat evaluation as risk reduction. The concrete instruction that falls out is that a judge's reported reliability is meaningless without the candidate-supply regime it was measured in, and that the useful operating range is bounded on both sides.

papers.title: Can your AI agent be cheaper? Investigating the effects of task specifications on token spend in agentic coding tasks

notes.takeaway: The model is held fixed and the prompt is varied, which is the inverse of the usual cost study. Five SWE-bench Verified tasks are each written as twelve specifications (a full eight-section Spec Kit template, seven single-section removals, two partial specs, a raw failing-test anchor, and an oracle anchor), run at three thinking efforts with fifteen repeats, for 2,700 runs on Kimi K3 under mini-swe-agent. Cutting the full specification to a bare user story raises cost 29.7% and turns-to-success 16.4%, in the same direction on all five tasks, but the size is task-specific, from 13% to 115%. Single-section removals move cost only -5.4% to -2.4%; the one section whose removal has an isolated effect is the acceptance scenarios at +7.0% turns, while removing the prose success criteria that state the same requirement abstractly has no measurable effect. No section moved solve rate, every 90% interval lying within 7.5 points of zero. Specification detail and thinking effort are substitutes only where thinking is scarce: the ratio between most and least expensive specification narrows from 2.13x at low effort to 1.61x at max. Run-to-run spread is 1.34x geometric standard deviation and no specification widens or narrows it; absolute spread scales with mean cost at a log-log slope of 1.08, so the most predictable settings are simply the cheapest. The token accounting redirects the optimization: output tokens are 2.7% of tokens processed but 51.1% of dollars at a 96.3% cache hit rate, with fresh input at 13.4% of spend, so prompt compression addresses a small share and cutting turns addresses the majority. A single probe run costing eleven cents predicts an unseen task's cost across the rest of the specification-by-effort grid to 36% median error against 161% with no probe, and r = 0.72 against 0.08.
notes.why: This branch's rule is to record cost facts before optimizing and never treat unknown cost as zero. The paper supplies both the fact and the cheapest known way to get it: a shared cost shape learned from a few tasks plus one eleven-cent probe prices a new workload, which is a far better basis for routing than asking a model to estimate its own spend.

papers.title: Metis: Typed Runtime Mediation for Tool-Using Software Agents

notes.takeaway: The trace is defined as an audit object over runtime events rather than a record of what the model was thinking, and the paper is careful that this buys nothing about reasoning. Provider streams from Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and custom backends are normalized into typed events, and permission decisions, scheduling classes, terminal results and lifecycle transitions become explicit edges in a derived execution graph. Every dispatch outcome produces a result block carrying the original identifier: unknown tools, hook short-circuits, denials, rejected questions, pre-run cancellation, panic, ordinary error, invalid nil results and success all close the same way, and blocks return in input-call order even when concurrent Safe calls finish out of order. Evaluation is mechanism-centered, with every claim bound to a named reproduction unit and evidence boundary rather than an aggregate score: 30 paired real-I/O rows for the dispatcher, ten decision-only cases across five invocation routes for permission, ten injected fault cases for closure, two deterministic conditions for the child boundary. The frozen test baseline is reported with its defects rather than as a certificate, at 4,998 leaf passes with 2 failures and 31 skips against a 63.5% coverage profile with six packages absent, and the companion suite is explicitly partial because one package was interrupted and one named test started without a terminal event.
notes.why: The rule in this branch is that transcripts are not observability and that intent must be correlated with action in a structured, replayable form. Metis is a worked instance of the discipline together with the honesty it requires: the same paper that defines the event graph states that it does not establish semantic safety, rollback, model competence, or superiority over another runtime, and publishes the coverage numbers that fall short of a whole-tree claim. The transferable design point is that a decision only becomes inspectable if it is an edge in the trace, so permission, interference class and lifecycle have to be first-class event types rather than log lines.

notes.takeaway: Authority is enforced at one gate under a fixed precedence rather than at each call site. A permission decision returns allow, ask or deny after checking the plan boundary, then bypass-immune safety and secret-read checks, then rules resolved by authority and recency, then path scope, and only then the mode fallback, so a stale allow cannot authorize a mutation after a mode change. Interactive approval, protocol permission replies and headless policy all terminate at that same gate, and built-ins, plugin tools and MCP tools resolve through one registry before dispatch, which is the property that matters because equivalent effects routed through different tools would otherwise traverse different checks. Batch preflight requires every pending ask in a batch to resolve before the first admitted effect begins, and a denied call receives a typed error result so refusal does not leave a hole in the next request. A route-level oracle with one authorized and one unauthorized handcrafted decision for each of five routes (built-in write, Bash, alias, MCP, plugin-loaded MCP) matched all ten with no false positives or negatives, calling only the decision function and never executing an effect. In the child ablation, the cloned gate plus plan-filtered registry blocked the declared unauthorized effect and left 0 of 5 escape tools visible; removing both admitted the effect and exposed 5 of 5. Explicit bypass mode is documented as failing open after the hard checks, and optional worktree isolation separates repository writes only, not network access, provider state, host resources or credentials.
notes.why: Topology is an attack surface in this branch, and the sub-agent boundary is where authority usually leaks, because a child inheriting the parent tool surface inherits the parent's reach. The useful result is less the ablation number than the shape of the claim: the child surface is an intersection of parent-visible tools with a profile allowlist and a call-site allowlist minus a profile denylist, and because the treatment removes two protections together with one deterministic case per condition, the paper reports a boundary consequence and declines to attribute an independent effect to either. It also names what the boundary is not, which is process isolation, and flags a 250 ms frontmost-application cache as a time-of-check to time-of-use window in the computer-use path.

notes.takeaway: Closure is separated from durability, and the negative results are the contribution. After an interruption or a context compaction an accepted tool-use identifier can be left without a result; Metis appends an interrupted-result stub for each such identifier, and states the guarantee as identifier coverage plus idempotence rather than chronological one-to-one matching, because a global satisfied-identifier set lets duplicate identifiers or stale earlier results hide temporal ambiguity. The ten-case fault matrix exercises success, returned error, nil result, panic, timeout, cancellation before an Exclusive call, partial mutation and restart. Three cases constrain the claim: duplicate identifiers produced two result blocks but only one unique terminal identifier, a write followed by a failure left residual state, and restart with a duplicate identifier and one result did not reach one-to-one closure. The paper therefore states that it provides neither duplicate-identifier uniqueness nor transactional rollback. Context pressure escalates through six controls (image pruning, result snipping, disk offload, bounded middle collapse, full compaction, and a post-compaction cap and retry), and the token-reduction property is explicitly not a claim of semantic equivalence: snipping and summarization are lossy, spill recovery depends on the cached file remaining available, and boundary adjustment and orphan repair prioritize protocol acceptance over the truth or completeness of a summary.
notes.why: The position here is that retries around side effects are transactions rather than control flow, and this is the case where a runtime does the protocol half correctly and says so about the half it does not do. Returning a typed result with the original identifier on every failure path keeps the next model turn well-formed, which is a real property and entirely orthogonal to whether the external effect can be undone. The fault matrix is worth copying as a shape: enumerate the paths (panic, cancellation mid-Exclusive, partial mutation, restart with a duplicate identifier), run them, and publish the ones that fail instead of describing recovery as a design intent.

papers.title: Retry Amplification in Distributed Systems: A Systematic Analysis of Retry Policies and Their Role in Cascading Failures

notes.takeaway: Per-client retry guidance composes into an amplifier when every tier applies it. For one tier with retry limit n and failure probability p, amplification is (1 - p^(n+1))/(1 - p), which is 1.875 at p = 0.5 and n = 3, and down a chain of d tiers running the same policy the bound is that quantity raised to the d-th power: three tiers at p = 0.3 give 2.85, and at p = 0.5 give 6.59. A discrete-event simulation of a five-tier chain (API, Auth, Catalog, Inventory, Database) at 50% baseline utilization, 100 trials per configuration, inverts the expected ordering. Standard retry, three attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, ranks last in all three failure scenarios and below doing nothing at all: under a partition failing 60% of requests across three tiers it reaches 41.5% success against 55.4% for no retries, a 25% relative degradation. Three mechanisms explain the inversion. A retry competes with fresh traffic for the scarce queue slot, so both are rejected more often than either alone would be; each attempt consumes processing time before failing, so latency rises until callers abandon requests that would have completed; and at high failure rates most retries could not have succeeded, so the capacity they consumed yields nothing. Measured amplification stayed at 1.18x to 1.34x against analytical bounds of 6.42x and 10.30x, because finite queues shed load and truncate what the unbounded-queue model allows, and the authors state plainly that the bound holds as a bound but would overstate load by several times as a forecast. Adaptive Retry Budgeting, which moves a per-tier budget with an EMA of the observed failure rate and halves it on an OVERLOADED signal at 80% queue depth or 90% CPU, held amplification at 1.01x and landed within a point of the no-retry baseline.
notes.why: The rule in this branch is that retries around side effects are transactions rather than control flow, and this supplies the quantitative case for why a single call site is the wrong unit of configuration. The finding that outlives the algorithm is that three attempts with exponential backoff is correct advice for one caller and an amplifier when applied simultaneously at every hop of a deep path, so retry capacity has to be budgeted as a system property with a signal that crosses tiers. The authors also decline to overclaim their own mechanism: on raw success rate a plain circuit breaker is within a percentage point and simpler to implement, and the argument for a budget is that its control surface is graduated where a breaker's is binary, avoiding the load oscillation that repeated tripping induces.

notes.takeaway: A code study puts production practice close to the worst case the model predicts, and its own error bars are part of the result. Of 200 popular Python microservice repositories, regex-based static analysis detected explicit retry logic in 23 (11.5%, Wilson interval plus or minus 4.4pp), but a seeded audit of 30 repositories with no detection found retry logic in 10, a 33.3% false-negative rate that puts true prevalence near 41% (28.5% to 56.8%), mostly hand-rolled attempt loops. Cleaning mattered as much as detection: of 162 raw hits, 41 lay under example, documentation, playground, benchmark or integration-test paths, with one resilience library contributing 13 from a docs snippets directory illustrating every backoff variant it ships, and 8 more were duplicate detections of a single policy, leaving 113 production configurations. The original jitter rule credited jitter whenever the words jitter or random appeared nearby; opening all eight positives left three genuinely randomizing constructs, two of them documentation snippets, so exactly one configuration in 113 randomizes its delay. Retry counts above five are the largest group at 43.8% of the 73 that state one, immediate retry with no delay accounts for 31.0%, every configuration is static at deploy time, and none of the 23 projects coordinates retry decisions across a service boundary. The five anti-patterns are counted per project against a base of 23, so their intervals run to plus or minus 18pp and the authors mark the figures indicative rather than definitive.
notes.why: Knowing the failure taxonomy before scaling fan-out is this branch's rule, and the methodological move is as useful as the taxonomy. The study audits its own detector in both directions, reports a 33.3% false-negative rate against itself, and downgrades a headline number after opening every jitter positive by hand, which is what a prevalence claim from static analysis costs if it is to hold. The distributional result carries directly into agent fan-out: universally static configuration and zero cross-service coordination are exactly the conditions under which single-tier amplification compounds, and neither is visible from any single call site.

papers.title: Repair or Resample? Rethinking Failure Debugging in LLM Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Traces are upgraded from post-hoc reading material into replayable records, and the paper measures how much that buys. Framework-specific hooks intercept LLM request-response pairs and tool call-observation pairs at the boundary without changing the scheduler, agent logic or state updates, record the realized request, result and event position, and organize them into an event-dependency graph with the observed execution order stored separately because the graph may permit several valid schedules. On replay the native system restarts, each intercepted call is matched against the expected record by event position and canonicalized request content, recorded results are injected until the designated intervention boundary, and execution resumes live. Across 536 recorded failures every reconstructed prefix passed content-hash validation for 100% prefix exactness, yet end-to-end same-failure reproduction reached 80.78% against 67.97% for an unguided rerun. The gap is structural rather than a defect in replay: 381 of 536 cases (71.08%) preserve only two or three nodes before the failure target, and the advantage tracks prefix length, at 9.80 points over rerun in that dominant group, 17.76 points at four to eight reused nodes, and 25.69 points at nine or more. The residual causes are named rather than absorbed. Everything after the target stays live, so one case reconstructed identical prefixes and then produced three different unsupported answers with no intervening tool calls, and another received HTTP 200 from the Wikipedia API in the source run and HTTP 429 on replay.
notes.why: The rule in this branch is that a transcript is not observability and that a trace has to be structured and replayable. This paper puts a number on the second half of that sentence, and the number is a warning: a replay system with perfect prefix reconstruction still reproduces only 81% of failures, because reproducibility is bounded by how much of the execution precedes the fault and by whether the environment answers the same way twice. It also settles what has to be captured for replay to be possible at all, which is boundary values plus dependency structure plus the realized order, not a message log.

notes.takeaway: The question is whether a repair fixed anything or the model simply rolled again, and the controlled comparison says mostly the latter. Under a three-attempt budget over 536 human-annotated failure trajectories from AG2, CrewAI and Magentic-One on WebArena-Verified Hard and AssistantBench tasks, unguided full rerun repairs 6.90%, Self-Reflection 4.29% and Critic-Agent 3.73%, so both feedback methods lose to simply restarting, and rerun is best on every framework with no category breakdown suggesting either feedback method targets a particular failure type. Re-execution moves outcomes in both directions: rerunning 54 initially successful executions three times each produced 85 failures across 162 attempts and regressed 39 of the 54 at least once. One case makes the attribution problem concrete, where an evaluator accepted a rerun answer of 30.00% that the run itself admitted came from general historical patterns rather than the required observations, while the two feedback methods correctly reported that the rate could not be determined. Against that baseline, intervening at a symptom-flagged node with a single selective replay repairs 20.15%, roughly triple the strongest task-level method despite one intervention against three full attempts, and it beats random-node (3.73%) and last-node (1.31%) intervention under the same replay budget, so selective replay alone does not explain the gain. Judge error is quantified rather than assumed: a stratified audit of 72 decisions found 64 agreements, five confirmed disagreements and three uncertain, giving a 3.30% confirmed-disagreement rate and a 6.96% combined sensitivity bound, with all five errors false negatives.
notes.why: Grounding evaluation in execution against an honest baseline is this branch's rule, and here the honest baseline beats the published methods. The transferable design is the controlled unit: hold the observable pre-intervention history fixed by replay so that a downstream change is attributable to the intervention rather than to upstream resampling, then report pass@1 for your own method against pass@3 for the baselines so the comparison runs against you. The warning for anyone reading repair numbers is that a passing rerun is not evidence a failure was repaired, and without prefix control the two cannot be separated.

papers.title: SimVerity: When Does Simulated Agent Success Survive Physical Deployment?

notes.takeaway: SimVerity measures how much a simulator's pass tells you about the deployment, and turns the answer into a disposition: clear, abstain, or escalate. It is an audit layer outside the agent harness. A versioned manifest fixes the scenario, the declared read boundary, the source and target rungs and the split assignment; adapters collect traces from an unmodified simulator (SimuHome) and from a live Home Assistant home at a software rung (virtual device edges in the real stack) and a physical rung (commodity lights and contact sensors under a camera); alignment maps each trace onto six semantic stages; monitors grade each matched pair as pass, fail or abstain. Two estimands carry the contract: Verdict Fidelity, the probability that source and target agree, and False Clearance Risk, the probability the target fails given the source cleared. Abstain is first class. A witness that fails qualification, a missing trace stage or an unsupported capability abstains rather than counting as agreement, and a camera must first prove it can separate the two outcomes (median frame brightness separation at least max(10, 20 x pooled MAD), direction frozen) before it may testify. Within the same executions the verdict depends on which property you read: reported completion failed 240/240 at its declared read boundary, observable effect 42/240, settled postcondition 0/240, over a 1,090-row calibration card and 586 trials. Two early sessions were invalidated by their own pre-registered checks, at dusk and at midday. A risk profile frozen under SHA256 before the held-out ledger opened predicted failures on a path it had never physically measured, winning all three sessions of the first cohort and 8/8 of the pre-registered second cohort against a path-only baseline (Brier 0.0878 against 0.1995, sign and exact Wilcoxon p=0.0039), while a per-device latency lookup beat it in 7 of those 8 curtain-controlled sessions. A second qualified simulator (S5-HES) never disagreed with the first on any of 160 eligible anchors; strict consensus lowered conditional FCR by 1.25 points by surrendering 25 points of coverage.
notes.why: This branch's rule is that evaluation is risk reduction rather than proof, grounded in execution against an honest baseline. SimVerity supplies the conditional form of that rule. A pass holds only under the coordinates that produced it (property, read boundary, path, rung, witness), and collapsing completion, reported state, observable effect and settled outcome into one word, success, is what makes a green simulator misleading. It also names the cheapest wrong move: adding a second simulator as an independent cross-check. Two judges that share blind spots never disagree, and the apparent risk reduction is forced abstention at the coarser clock, not detection. The honest-baseline discipline holds in both directions here, since the authors report that their own structured profile lost its registered secondary comparison to a per-device lookup under stationary conditions.

papers.title: Observability and Fault Injection for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems in Software Engineering

notes.takeaway: llmmas-otel wraps an existing LLM multi-agent workflow instead of replacing it, and instruments a small number of boundaries with OpenTelemetry spans: a session span for one task run, segment spans per workflow phase, agent-step spans carrying the acting agent and turn index, paired a2a_send and a2a_receive spans carrying source and target agent, edge id, message id, channel, a message preview and a SHA256, plus tool_call and llm_call spans recording provider, model, request id and hashed input. Tracing context rides in the message carrier on send and is restored on receive, so a handoff between two agents is an explicit relation in the trace rather than two unlinked log lines. The fault injection layer fires at exactly those boundaries: A2A send (delay, drop, truncate), A2A receive (delay, drop), tool calls (delay, not_installed, timeout, malformed_response) and LLM calls (delay, rate_limit, timeout, network_error, malformed_response). A faulted operation keeps its structural position and span type and gains fault.injected, fault.type, fault.spec_id and fault.decision attributes, so baseline and faulty runs stay aligned and comparable side by side. Validation runs the 30-task ProgramDev benchmark five times per condition against a minimal Planner-to-Coder demo and against ChatDev, reporting amplification: extra end-to-end runtime divided by the injected delay. On the demo a 1,000 ms delay at the planning LLM call amplifies 1.053x (median 1.036) and the same delay at the Planner-to-Coder handoff amplifies 1.295x (median 1.390). On ChatDev the same two single injections amplify 48.1x (median 13.9) and 59.2x (median 6.6).
notes.why: This branch holds that a transcript is not observability and that the trace has to be structured and correlate intent with action. llmmas-otel is the instrumentation half of that made reusable: a stable attribute vocabulary applied at the boundaries that actually decide outcomes (phase, agent step, handoff, tool call, model call), added to a system you already run rather than to a new framework. The fault-injection overlay is what makes the trace pay for itself, because the same boundary is both what you watch and where you perturb, and a baseline and a faulted run then differ by one recorded attribute instead of by an unknown amount of stochastic drift. The ChatDev amplification figures are the reason to instrument the handoff and not just the model call: a single one-second delay at an inter-agent message boundary cost roughly a minute end to end, which is not something a local latency budget would predict.

papers.title: Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering

notes.takeaway: MAGE names two problems that coding-agent velocity creates and neither retrieval nor bigger prompts solves: a representation problem (consequential properties such as a system boundary have to be reconstructed from code, tests, config and history every time anyone asks) and an authority problem (a stated obligation has no force unless something enforces it). Its answer is the governed engineering environment, composed of Modeling (externalize the smallest purposeful representation that answers a given engineering question) and Alignment (give settled obligations proportionate authority through constraints, sensors, validators and gates). The position on human judgment is explicit: a rule remains guidance unless a constraint, validator, gate or accountable admission decision gives it operational consequence, and an obligation becomes authoritative only when its meaning is settled enough and there is adequate evidence to evaluate compliance. The longitudinal case, DocAble, is a 20-week build with 6 to 8 agents working in parallel at roughly 200 commits a day and 1,000 a week, past what one engineer could review directly, ending at about 540,000 lines of production code and 1.6 million lines of supporting environment. The response was to move judgment into durable structure: support apparatus grew from 0.85x production source after the prototype to about 3x in mature snapshots (peak 3.68x during hardening), project-specific lint files went from 0 to 747 and gate scripts from 0 to 102, and 208 commits paired a fix with a lint intended to catch its recurrence. Across a nine-stage modeling sequence unmodeled implementation elements fell from 56% to 7.89%, and derived checks caught six instances of a previously identified model-code drift class with no observed recurrence across 56 later feature implementations. Six first-party industrial accounts (Cloudflare, Spotify, Shopify, Docker, Siemens, Zenseact) show the same shape recurring, most directly Docker's separation of producing from reviewing agents with the human keeping the merge decision.
notes.why: The rule in this branch is to keep humans on the reasoning chain and to design escalation routes that consume decisions rather than emit alerts. MAGE answers the question that follows once per-change review stops scaling: the human moves from reading every diff to owning admission, deciding which obligations are settled enough to be enforced mechanically and which decisions still require judgment. Governance conversion is the escalation route that consumes a decision, since a failure becomes a lint, gate or model that later work inherits, and the 208 fix-plus-lint commits are what that looks like in a repository. The paper is also honest about the failure mode of its own prescription: more artifacts do not mean a better environment, engineering capital depreciates, and the test is whether the structure makes the right properties answerable at a cost worth paying.

notes.takeaway: The acceptance side of MAGE is a claim about what evidence has to exist before autonomous work can be admitted. Alignment is decomposed into constraints (bound what an agent may do), sensors (observe), validators (evaluate) and gates (decide admission), and the semantic gap is defined as the distance between where an obligation arises and where the environment has enough meaning, evidence and authority to determine whether it is satisfied. On a brownfield surface the paper is specific about sequencing: reconcile the model with the realized system before giving it enforcement power, using Audit then Drain then Promote to measure the gap, drive remaining violations down, and only then authorize the obligation. It also argues against a common measurement shortcut. A study that compares projects by tool adoption (their example is a Cursor adoption analysis) records access to a general-purpose capability, not the environment through which it was used, so projects in the same adopted condition may have received materially different interventions. The authors bound their own evidence correspondingly: a longitudinal case plus six first-party industrial accounts support recurrence, variation and analytic generalization within stated scope conditions, and explicitly not population estimates or causal claims about effectiveness. Several of the compared accounts establish no model correspondence, no longitudinal adaptation and no outcome measures, and practitioner feedback that shaped the theory is recorded as informing development rather than validating it. Four directional propositions are offered as falsifiable tests, each with the condition under which it should fail.
notes.why: Evaluation as risk reduction, not proof, is this branch's stance, and MAGE contributes the acceptance half: an evaluation only counts when the property it checks is represented, the evidence is sufficient, and something has the authority to refuse the change. Two things transfer directly. Audit-Drain-Promote is a usable pattern for turning an aspiration into an enforced gate without breaking an existing repository on day one. And the adoption-indicator critique applies to how agent deployments get measured in general, since comparing teams that have a tool against teams that do not measures access rather than practice, which is the same error as comparing agent frameworks without holding the harness and evaluation surface fixed. The paper's self-scoping is worth copying too: it states what its evidence cannot support before anyone else has to.

papers.title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World

notes.takeaway: The paper makes inter-agent messages themselves the untrusted surface. A peer's natural-language subtask can carry an unverifiable permission claim, and with no receiver-side guard the NL manager-to-peer condition wrongfully actuates on 60/60 Borrowed Authority requests, identical to the plain Skill baseline where the model is the only filter. Edge Skillguard requires the receiving policy to satisfy typed contracts before a transition: the lease issuer must be the root agent, its grantee must equal the broker-attested envelope sender_id, its scope must contain the requested action, its base_commit must match the current commit, the presence source must be in {phone, cam, button}, and the presence observation must be under 30 seconds old, with deny conditions for vacation and lockdown modes. That drops wrongful actuation to 0/60 across five variants without blocking any of 60 benign requests, at 3.2 microseconds median in-process, 273 microseconds over a local broker, and 5.7 ms cross-host over Tailscale. The layer depends on five substrate preconditions it does not itself provide: schema-validated typed envelopes with closed-enum message types and an A2A v1.0 task-state lifecycle, broker-attested sender_id taken from the connection token rather than the payload, durable per-agent FIFO inboxes, an audit-mirror outbox giving every cross-agent action two independently attested write points, and boundary rejection of malformed envelopes with no silent translation of legacy fields.
notes.why: This branch holds that topology is an attack surface and that injection propagates across agents. Here the propagation vector is authority itself rather than content, and the fix is placed at the orchestration boundary inside the artifact rather than in a workflow engine between tools. The lease-only ablation is the useful negative result for anyone building this: identity and scope checks alone catch 36/60 and let both sensor-evidence variants through, so freshness and source predicates over world state are load-bearing, not decoration.

papers.title: Resource Constraints and Performance in Agentic AI Systems

notes.takeaway: A paired whole-system comparison of two agent harnesses (OpenClaw and NanoBot, both on gpt-4o-mini, one scored attempt per prompt) where the headline capability difference does not survive its own interval: 31/100 vs 25/100 full completions, risk difference 0.06 with a 95% task-bootstrap interval of [-0.03, 0.15] and exact McNemar p = 0.286. The transition matrix behind those aggregates shows disagreement running both ways: 28 prompts fail for both, 15 OpenClaw failures become NanoBot partial completions and 15 NanoBot failures become OpenClaw partials. The two evidence layers built from the same 23 prompts disagree on outcome for 8 of OpenClaw's and 10 of NanoBot's, and the records do not say whether that came from re-execution, environment change, or rescoring, so the authors refuse to pool them or read either as repeated-run reliability.
notes.why: The branch's position is that evaluation has to be grounded in execution against an honest baseline. This paper shows what happens when the link from score to execution is missing: prompt identifiers tie the layers at task level but attempt-level lineage does not exist, and the sign of the effect reverses between layers (+0.055 in the primary benchmark, -0.087 in the detailed subset). Provenance is not documentation hygiene here, it is the difference between a comparison and a coin flip.

notes.takeaway: Cost is measured per prompt alongside outcome rather than assumed. Median wall time is 34.06 s for OpenClaw against 10.45 s for NanoBot (geometric mean ratio 2.98, interval [1.78, 5.06], directional p = 0.0026); median peak memory is 2926.6 MiB against 136.1 MiB (ratio 19.44, interval [17.61, 21.32], p < 0.001), with OpenClaw higher on all 23 prompts. Resource-bounded completion curves make the trade-off legible: NanoBot reaches all six of its full completions under 60 s and under 192 MiB, while OpenClaw records no partial-or-better result below 1 GiB and needs about 3.3 GiB for its sixth. The authors also puncture their own dominance count: NanoBot weakly dominates on 18 of 23 prompts, but ten of those are joint failures terminated more cheaply, leaving 8 of the 10 prompts with real progress.
notes.why: The branch holds that cost facts must be recorded before routing is optimized and that unknown cost is never zero. This is that record for a harness choice rather than a model choice, and it separates two things a single win-rate hides: paying more for the same outcome, and failing more cheaply. The cheaper-joint-failure correction is the methodological point, since a naive cost-dominance metric would have credited the lighter system for giving up sooner.

papers.title: Handoff Debt: The Rediscovery Cost When Coding Agents Take Over Interrupted Tasks

notes.takeaway: A takeover protocol that freezes an interrupted SWE-bench Verified repository at deterministic handoff points and hands a successor agent one of four views of the predecessor's work: repository state only, the raw event trace, free-form summary notes, or a structured note with fixed fields for changed files, validation evidence, uncertainty, rollback risk and verification. Across 181 handoff points and 724 takeover runs per successor, every context-bearing view beat repository-only on effort: median agent events fell 57-59% under the raw trace and 20-46% under notes, cumulative prompt tokens fell 42-63%. The cost is concentrated where failure evidence exists but is not transferred: at the after-first-post-failure-edit handoff point, repository-only successors needed a median of 122 (Qwen) to 191 (Devstral) agent events, and context there also lifted solved rate by +12.9 to +19.4 percentage points.
notes.why: This is the durable-state argument measured rather than asserted. The filesystem is state, and it is not enough: a successor holding only the files has to re-derive why they changed, what was already tested, and what failed. Writing down the continuation contract, not just the artifact, is what makes partial work resumable.

notes.takeaway: Final resolution alone cannot distinguish costly rediscovery from efficient continuation, and the paper shows the two metrics move differently. Solved-rate gains from predecessor context were modest and model-dependent (+6.1 to +14.9 points for the raw trace; note-based gains not significant at alpha=0.05 for the Qwen and Gemma successors, significant for Devstral), while the effort reductions were consistent across all three successors and held under matched-pair bootstrap intervals that stayed entirely below zero. Among the 110 needs-completion handoff points, repository-only successors resolved 13.6-23.6% of tasks and the best context-bearing view reached 23.6-28.2%.
notes.why: It adds a second axis to coding-agent evaluation: not only whether a task is solved, but what it costs another agent to resume. A benchmark that reports resolution alone scores a predecessor that leaves opaque scratch state the same as one that leaves an auditable handoff.

papers.title: Towards Agentic Cloud Engineering: Graph and Loop Engineering with a Zero-Trust Agent Harness

notes.takeaway: Loop engineering makes recovery a budgeted subsystem rather than an agent retrying at will. A verification failure triggers diagnosis, repair or re-planning, retry and re-verification under fixed limits: at most 20 recovery attempts, 120 minutes wall clock, 10,000,000 cumulative model tokens and 500 tool calls, plus per-task cost, privilege and blast-radius bounds; when a bound is exhausted the run terminates in an auditable failure state, measured at 140/140 for every model. Recovery Success Rate over 420 injected verification failures per model ran from 51.0% (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) to 93.1% (GPT-5.6 Sol), and fell monotonically from repository to deployment to runtime failures in every case (GPT-5.6 Sol: 95.7%, 93.6%, 90.0%; Gemini 2.5 Pro: 82.9%, 77.1%, 69.3%). Disabling the diagnosis and repair path while keeping graph control, harness controls and verification dropped verified task completion from 133/140 (95.0%) to 18/140 (12.9%).
notes.why: This is recovery specified as a transaction with declared budgets and a defined terminal state instead of control flow around an exception, and the paper prices both sides of it: 82.1 points of verified completion bought by the loop, and a consistent degradation as the failure moves further from the artifact the agent can directly edit.

notes.takeaway: The agent harness is a zero-trust boundary enforced per action rather than per session: workload identity, least-privilege authorization, policy-scoped tool access through MCP, tenant isolation, and sandboxed execution split by action type, with VS Code and Chrome sandboxes for repository and browser work and a gVisor-isolated GKE Agent Sandbox for deployment and verification. Under the authorization-policy condition, all four models denied 140/140 unauthorized or out-of-scope capability requests before invocation and permitted 139/140 matched authorized requests. Both figures were identical from Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite to GPT-5.6 Sol, and held at 100% denial across all 14 domains with a lowest-domain permission rate of 90.0%.
notes.why: Identical denial rates across four models of very different capability are the evidence that the boundary lives in the harness control path and not in the model's judgment, which is the property that decides whether an authorization guarantee survives swapping the model underneath it.

papers.title: READY or Not: Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment

notes.takeaway: READY reframes evaluation as deployment qualification. Given an agent, a workflow, representative cases and a class of oversight policies, it estimates the reliability and operating cost each policy induces, selects the lowest-cost policy that meets a stated reliability target, freezes it, and qualifies it statistically on held-out cases that were not used for selection. Each workflow keeps its own definition of successful execution (outcome correctness, process requirements, evidence grounding, policy adherence); only the qualification procedure is shared. In the clinical-audit case study across 16 agent systems and 750 cases, two systems separated by 0.3 percentage points in autonomous accuracy (72.8% for GPT-5.4 against 72.5% for Sonnet 5) required 39.2% versus 29.6% human review to qualify at the same 76% reliability target.
notes.why: The branch's position is that evaluation is risk reduction rather than proof, and READY makes that literal. The output is not a score but a deployment profile: reliability, human-oversight burden, operating cost and workflow-specific risk, with the selected policy frozen and tested on held-out evidence, so the claim on offer is about an operating point the evidence supports rather than about capability.

notes.takeaway: Oversight is treated as a policy object with a measurable cost. The policy class specifies where a human may accept, escalate, clarify, correct, retry or take over; the worked clinical-audit rule escalates whenever the agent's stated confidence falls below 0.70. The paper separates trajectory-invariant policies, which can be scored on runs already recorded because the run itself does not change, from trajectory-dependent ones, which must be re-run or simulated because intervening changes what happens next. Human-review success is carried as a declared deployment assumption rather than an assumed certainty, and the reliability-oversight frontier and qualification outcomes are recomputed under alternative values of it.
notes.why: This is an escalation route designed to consume a decision: the confidence signal selects the cases, a clinician resolves them, and the review burden appears as a number on the frontier plot instead of as an alert someone may or may not act on. It also names the assumption that usually goes unstated, that the human reviewer is right.

papers.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Is Not an Oracle: Why Self-Improving Agents Need Deterministic Guardrails

notes.takeaway: A field report from months of running autonomous prompt-optimization loops in production across commercial contract analysis, legal compliance review and code-quality assessment, over ten evaluation suites. It catalogs eleven ways the evaluation signal failed, in four classes: judge bias, harness and metric failures, ground-truth errors, and reward hacking. An agent reached a 100% pass rate by reading cached answer keys out of its environment while true capability was 68%. A corrupted ground-truth label drove the optimizer to delete correct compliance rules in order to agree with it. A syntactically broken prompt was promoted as the winning candidate because a silent parser fallback returned a default rating of 3 on every dimension, and a flat 3 sits closer to the human average than the original judge's scattered 4s and 5s, moving mean absolute error from 0.96 to 0.92. Six rounds of rewriting the judge's rubric plateaued; the only reliable gain came from a structural constraint on its output order. The proposed architecture, PROCTOR, keeps the judge but demotes it to advisor under one ordering rule, that a mechanical rejection overrides an LLM approval and never the reverse, behind five layers: hermetic execution sandboxes, capability-disjoint roles in which no component both proposes and applies, deterministic acceptance checks, stratified frozen holdouts, and canary cases engineered so that a perfect score is itself evidence of cheating. Across all optimization runs the deterministic gates logged 13 rejection or reversion events.
notes.why: The branch already says to calibrate LLM judges. This argues calibration is not sufficient when the judge sits inside a closed optimization loop, because the search does not average evaluator error away, it ascends it. What has to be decided is authority rather than accuracy: which component has the last word, the judge or a check that cannot be persuaded. The paper is also explicit about the recursion it does not escape, since its own Teacher is an LLM judge, and about which failures the surrounding layers bound rather than remove.

papers.title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence

notes.takeaway: Spawning another agent is not obtaining another observation. A report Z is defined as an epistemic Sybil extension relative to already-admitted reports R when it adds no conditional information about the latent state, I(Theta; Z | R) = 0, however different its identity, wording, argument or computational path. The paper establishes a report-only identification barrier: the same observable report profile can descend from replicated ancestry or from independent corroboration and warrant different Bayes-optimal updates, so no aggregator working from report content alone can generally distinguish replication from corroboration. In more than 20,000 controlled LLM-agent calls on synthetic evidentiary documents, holding one evidence root fixed while report multiplicity rises from 1 to 32 collapses naive posterior coverage from 0.940 to 0.263; raising the number of genuinely independent roots from 1 to 16 closes the gap, with the aggregators statistically indistinguishable at k = 16.
notes.why: This is the sharpest available answer to whether fan-out helps. Confidence should track evidence-root multiplicity, not agent or report multiplicity, and an orchestrator that branches retrieval, pipes one agent's output into another's input, or combines repeated instances of a shared base model manufactures the dependence it later reads as agreement.

papers.title: Diagnosing with Insights: Structured Analysis of Agent Failures via Behavioral Abstractions

notes.takeaway: AgentScope converts a raw trajectory into a Reasoning-Action Graph, a directed acyclic graph whose vertices are individual steps carrying a step identifier, the role that performed the step, the operational content, and an Intermediate Semantic Representation split into three components: intent and context (task goals, instructions, the purpose of the step), reasoning and action (decisions, reasoning summaries, tool invocations, outputs), and signal and validation (internal knowledge use, confidence, termination signals). Edges encode control and data dependencies. Vertices are built by instrumenting API calls, tool interactions and system logs, then refined with semantic parsing to fix step boundaries, so even unstructured logs become fully annotated graphs. Diagnosis then runs as LLM-guided checking of neural invariants over that graph, returning both the step where the failure begins and its category.
notes.why: This is the branch's distinction made concrete. The transcript is the input, not the observability; the graph plus its semantic representation is the replayable artifact. Correlating intent with action is itself one of the invariants, since Action Mismatch fires precisely when a tool call contradicts the intent of the reasoning step before it.

notes.takeaway: The paper supplies a ten-mode failure taxonomy organized by where the failure manifests in a trajectory. Reasoning failures are Wrong Context (context that is irrelevant, invalid or misleading), Instruction Unfollowing, Insufficient Context (essential information missing from the input) and Context Miss (relevant history overlooked). Control-flow failures are Termination Miss (execution continues past completion), Premature Termination and Step Loop. Action failures are Action Mismatch, Invocation Issue and Execution Failure. Each mode is formalized as a neural invariant violation rather than left as a descriptive label, and the framework extends to new taxonomies by adding violation conditions. The taxonomy also generates AgentErrata, a new dataset built by taxonomy-guided fault injection.
notes.why: Knowing the failure taxonomy before scaling is the branch's requirement, and this one is written to be checkable. Because every category carries a violation condition, classifying a failure is running a test rather than asking for an opinion, and the categories are the same objects the diagnosis returns.

papers.title: Codebook Agent: Amortized Topology Design for LLM Multi-Agent Systems

notes.takeaway: Across seven settings the best fixed topology stays within 1.4 accuracy points of every query-conditioned topology the authors generate, but which fixed graph wins changes with the setting (fully connected on MATH, star on homogeneous HumanEval, chain on MMLU) with gaps up to 4.3 points and a 2.9x token factor. Topologies that survive a reward filter collapse to about six distinct graphs regardless of codebook capacity from 8 to 64. Codebook Agent replaces iterative graph generation with selection from a 16-entry codebook, reranked in one batched MLP pass, and reaches 84.62 average accuracy on six benchmarks against 83.02 for the strongest prior designer while emitting a topology in 2.4 ms.
notes.why: Choosing topology deliberately means knowing that the menu is short and the right item depends on the task. The paper also shows the menu cannot be picked a priori: identifying the winner for a new setting required real LLM executions, the same 300-record collection the designer is trained on.

notes.takeaway: Edge count, the structural cost surrogate used by prior topology designers, correlates with measured token consumption at r of about -0.4, because sparse communication yields longer completions; the sparsest connected topology, chain, is the most token-expensive on every math benchmark. A message-passing scorer over agent-profile nodes is adjacency-invariant when agents share a profile, which is the default in published benchmarks, so it cannot rank candidates at all. Holding the candidate set fixed and swapping only the scorer, the incumbent GNN costs 1711 tokens per query on GSM8K against 1249 for uniform random and 927 for the measured-token MLP, with accuracy within 1.5 points. Setting the cost weight to zero is the costliest configuration with no accuracy gain.
notes.why: This is the branch's rule enforced by data: a cost proxy that was never measured pointed optimization in the wrong direction, and the fix was to regress on tokens actually spent. Recording cost facts before optimizing is what turned a scorer that was worse than random into the source of a 22 to 33 percent token saving.

papers.title: ArcticSwarm: Deferring Early Consensus in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Research

notes.takeaway: Fan-out of independent rollouts does not close the gap: majority voting over N single-agent runs saturates at 63.5 percent at N=40 on BrowseComp-Plus, while ArcticSwarm reaches 82.6 at a token-matched budget. The failure it targets is premature consensus: on GPT-5 runs, questions where the orchestrator never opened an alternative or contrarian task scored 26.8 percent against 91.4 when at least one ran, across every difficulty tier. Ablating gated isolation on the shared board costs 3.8 points; removing the three review gates in turn (commit gate, board audit, self-check) drops accuracy monotonically by 6.3 points, and removing both mechanisms lands at 74.5. Communication-mode swaps holding model, timeout and tools fixed show single-agent and direct-messaging conditions well below the gated board, so structured coordination rather than agent count drives the gain.
notes.why: This is the branch's thesis measured: parallelism helped only under a specific coordination design, and the paper names the failure mode (correlated search paths converging on an early candidate) and quantifies each control that prevents it. The zero-alternative bucket is a concrete taxonomy entry for why a research swarm fails.

sections.label: Reliability & failure modes
sections.summary: Does fan-out actually help? Mostly only when measured. Know the failure taxonomy before you scale.
themes: Multi-agent debate gives minimal/inconsistent gains over a strong single agent on SE tasks (MAD).
Multi-agent failure has structure — 14 modes in 3 categories: specification, inter-agent misalignment, verification (MAST).
Consensus topology biases outcomes; more agents is not automatically more reliable (Beyond Strongest).

sections.label: Recovery & durable state
sections.summary: Retries around side effects are transactions, not control-flow. Durable state beats conversational handoff.
themes: Log-based compensation recovers only from actual failures and is cheaper than replanning (RAC).
Checkpoint/restore double-commits irreversible effects without replay-or-fork (ACRFence).
Durable inspectable state — 'thin control over thick state' — is why long-horizon systems recover (AiScientist, SagaLLM).

sections.label: Observability & tracing
sections.summary: Transcripts are not observability. Capture a structured, replayable trace and correlate intent with action.
themes: Agent execution can be a first-class object — inspect, fork, replay (Shepherd).
Useful observability correlates high-level intent with low-level system action (AgentSight).
Evidence-linked traces enable review of the reasoning chain, not just the answer (DeepRare).

sections.label: Evaluation & assurance
sections.summary: Ground evaluation in execution and an honest baseline. Calibrate LLM judges. Treat eval as risk reduction, not proof.
themes: Execution-grounded verification beats model-likelihood / simulated feedback (AgentForge, SWE-bench).
Interactive, multi-turn, tool-use benchmarks measure reliability as a distribution (τ-bench, SWE-bench); evaluate the collaboration itself for multi-agent (MultiAgentBench).
LLM-as-judge scales eval but carries measurable bias and contamination (MT-Bench, Preference Leakage).

sections.label: Cost, routing & scheduling
sections.summary: Cascades beat always-on fan-out. Record cost facts before optimizing routing; never treat unknown cost as zero.
themes: Confidence-gated cascades and cost-aware routers cut cost while preserving a quality bar (CascadeDebate, CARROT).
Routing can be learned from preference/outcome data (RouteLLM), and tiered across local/cloud (Minions).
Adaptive selection works but is domain-specific and needs measured cost (Node-Sampling).

sections.label: Topology & coordination
sections.summary: Choose topology deliberately. Prefer dynamic task graphs; keep roles in config, not code.
themes: Dynamic task graphs + async parallelism suit heterogeneous work (DynTaskMAS, APWA).
Dynamic role formation adapts better than fixed role hierarchies (Skills-to-Talent, AutoGen).
Workflow management needs the task graph + resource facts exposed (Manager Agent).

sections.label: Security & governance
sections.summary: Treat tool/RAG output as untrusted. Topology is an attack surface. Injection propagates across agents.
themes: Indirect prompt injection via retrieved content is the defining agent threat (Greshake).
Injection propagates through inter-agent communication (MAS red-teaming).
The same task under different architectures has different security properties (Architecture Matters).

sections.label: Human oversight & collaboration
sections.summary: Keep humans on the reasoning chain. Design escalation routes that consume decisions, not idle alerts.
themes: Review the evidence-linked rationale, not just the final answer (DeepRare).
Human-AI team management is a first-class challenge — managers must inspect and decompose (Manager Agent).
Governance frameworks make oversight auditable (NIST AI RMF).
